2109454493415023080.prompt:
Edit my talking-head video into a polished YouTube video with explanatory motion graphics.

INPUT
- Raw video: <path/to/raw.mp4>. Speech is Portuguese; don't translate.
- Target: at most <6:30>. Style: premium, clean, editorial ("Anthropic/Apple level").
- End card: subscribe + follow me on X (<https://x.com/handle>) + "comment what you want to see next".
- Never cover my face. Never show where I live.

STACK
- Remotion (https://remotion.dev/) for the composition, ffmpeg for cuts and encoding, Python for analysis.
- Transcribe with word timestamps using ElevenLabs Scribe. It has precise word boundaries and marks fillers like "hã"/"é".
- If you use Whisper instead: its word ends stretch over pauses, so refine every cut point with the audio energy.

1) PLAN THE CUT
- Make an indexed transcript (word index → text, start, end).
- Choose keep-ranges by word index. Remove fillers, false starts, repeated sentences and weak tangents until it fits the target.
- Put the strongest line (2–4 s) at the very start as a cold-open hook.

2) CUT, FRAME-ACCURATE AND IN SYNC
- Cut points:
- Cut in the silence between words, never inside a word.
- Keep ~50 ms before the first word and ~60 ms after the last word (~160 ms if it ends a sentence).
- Silences inside kept ranges:
- Detect them with a 10 ms RMS envelope. A threshold around −38 dBFS worked here; measure your own noise floor first.
- Shorten any pause over 0.32 s to 0.22 s (0.36 s after a sentence ends).
- Round every boundary to whole frames (30 fps) and merge touching segments.
- Video: ffmpeg split → trim(start_frame, end_frame) → concat, plus a light grade (hqdn3d, eq, colorbalance, unsharp) → intermediate at CRF 14.
- Audio: cut the same boundaries in numpy with 8 ms fades and no overlap. A/V stays in sync.
- QA: re-transcribe the cut and diff it against the intended text. Fix leaked fragments and clipped word starts, then repeat until clean.

3) FACE TRACK
- Detect the face every 0.2 s (Apple Vision or MediaPipe).
- Smooth with a moving average inside each cut segment, never across a jump cut.
- Use it to frame the camera and to place graphics on the side away from the face.

4) DESIGN SYSTEM
- One palette: dark warm stage #14120F, ivory "paper" #F1ECE2, one accent (clay #D97A4E).
- Fonts: Fraunces (serif display), Inter Tight (UI), JetBrains Mono (labels). Add subtle grain and soft glows.
- No gradient text, no neon.
- Camera layout modes, morphing between them in ~0.7 s (cubic in-out):
- full frame;
- split left/right: rounded camera card 856×936, face at 42% of its height, graphics on the other half;
- PIP: 256 px circle over a full-screen paper sheet, for chapter moments.

5) BEAT SHEET (JSON)
- Give every sentence group a visual, cued to word start times in the cut timeline:
- lower third (name/role);
- big numbers with count-up;
- lists that reveal on each spoken item;
- SVG diagrams that draw on;
- timeline, before→after, comparison cards, quotes;
- arrows annotating objects in the room.
- Structure: cold open with kinetic captions → 1.5 s title card → content → end card (CTAs plus a portrait still).

6) BUILD IN REMOTION
- One composition, 1920×1080 at 30 fps. Put `<OffthreadVideo>` (muted) inside a container whose rect and transform come from the layout keyframes plus the face track.
- Each graphic is a `<Sequence>` component. Drive reveals with useCurrentFrame + interpolate/spring (opacity, translateY, blur).
- SVG draw-on: animate strokeDashoffset using the real path length.
- Jump cuts: alternate zoom 1.0 ↔ 1.075 around the face when the picture jumps. Add a 1–2% slow breathing zoom elsewhere and a punch-in on punchlines.
- Deterministic only: no Math.random.
- Check key frames with `npx remotion still`: face uncovered, no clipped text, nothing appearing before its cue.

7) SOUND
- Voice: highpass 80 Hz, light denoise, −2.5 dB at 280 Hz, +2 dB at 3.6 kHz, de-ess, 3:1 compressor.
- Music: royalty-free lo-fi (e.g. Mixkit). Change track per section with 4 s crossfades.
- Duck 9–12 dB under the voice in the speech band, keeping the lows.
- Louder only on the title and end cards.
- SFX: very subtle whooshes on layout changes, pops on reveals, ticks on counters.
- Master: two-pass loudnorm to −14 LUFS, true peak −1.5.

8) RENDER, VERIFY, DELIVER
- Encode: H.264 CRF 16, AAC 320k, BT.709, +faststart.
- Verify:
- duration within the target, −14 LUFS;
- no frozen stretch over 0.3 s;
- a 40-frame contact sheet;
- re-transcribe the final mix: at least 95% of words should match, so the music isn't masking the voice.
- Deliver the MP4, an .srt from the word timings (max 42 chars per line, 2 lines), and YouTube chapters (first at 0:00, each at least 10 s).

RULES
- Show numbers and claims exactly as I say them.
- Check names and spellings on the web before they go on screen.
- No invented stats or testimonials.
- Short, concrete on-screen copy with no AI clichés.
- Don't publish anything without my OK.

2117987052419428576.prompt:
Create a 2D anime short for the web. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Deliver the final result as a single, self-contained HTML file that plays offline, with a synthesized soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything etc.

Use theatrical mecha and kaiju anime as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color, and atmosphere. The film is 83 seconds long, in 39 shots. Its characters are a colossal silver archer robot, a fleet of container ships, and a leviathan. No people appear in the film. Use any tools or techniques you want, including 3D, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

SCENE

A blazing sunny day on a coast. A massive armored archer robot, a hundred meters tall, stands in a deep lunge on a headland and draws a bow taller than itself. Close-ups: the hand on the grip, the limb and cable, the foot planted in the surf. Blue energy crawls along the arrow into the chest armor until the arrowhead blazes like crystal. The string snaps forward and a shockwave flattens the sea. The arrow is a harpoon trailing a thin cable. It tears the clouds into two walls above a ship's deck, climbs through the cloud tops, and reaches the edge of space in a blue flash along the planet's limb.

Out at sea, container ships cross a colossal shadow. Four humpback whales breach beside a ship, with real arcs and full tail flukes, and dive tail last. From below, shapes move under the bright churning surface. Four whale heads rise from a boiling sea, and a ring of teeth rises around them: they are lures inside a mouth. They drop in and the jaws shut. The leviathan breaches through the fleet in one slow, enormous arc. Its belly slides past the bridge windows. The swell it leaves lifts the ships and stands one on end, spilling containers. Its ridged back and flukes sink into spray fog.
High above, the arrow turns over and comes back red-hot through the atmosphere. Below the surface, the leviathan crawls through a luminous canyon on clawed forelimbs and swallows a fleeing whale. A thin streak meets the sea on the horizon and a white plume swells up. The harpoon drives through its back in a blue-white flash, lightning runs along its body, and the barbed tip punches out of its belly into the rock, which bursts apart. The cable stays attached the whole time, rising to the surface. A mountain of water swells from the sea. The dying leviathan erupts, rolls over between the ships and falls, and a wall of water takes the fleet.

ANIME QUALITY STANDARD

Every frame must look as if it was drawn by professional anime animators and painted by master background artists for a finished theatrical film.

Archer: A massive, heavy anime mecha with sculpted overlapping armor plates, panel lines, bolts, markings and a faceted chest reactor that glows blue. Hands really grip the bow and string. The arrow never passes through the armor. Keep it on-model from every angle.

Leviathan: Whale-like and colossal, always dwarfing the ships. Rough, dark grey-teal wet hide with barnacles and scars, a pale ribbed throat, a spined back, huge clawed flippers, and a cavernous maw with uneven teeth. A real bending body with weight, never a stiff model hanging on pillars of water.
Whales: Real humpback anatomy with tail stock, big notched flukes and long curved flippers rooted in the body.

Ships: Detailed container ships with corrugated multicolor containers, lashing bars and a white bridge tower.

Line art: Confident, delicate, hand-inked anime line work with subtle variation in thickness and pressure.
Coloring: Traditional anime cel coloring with clean color areas, hard-edged cool lavender-blue shadows, crisp highlights, and a bright, high-key, saturated palette. Never gloomy, grey or muddy, even in the darkest moments of the story.

Backgrounds: Richly detailed, hand-painted anime backgrounds in a gouache style: towering white cumulus, a cobalt-to-turquoise sea at kilometer scale, a painted coast with a far town, Earth from orbit, a port city from the stratosphere.

Underwater: Luminous cyan depth with god rays, a rippling surface seen from below, jagged canyon rock, silt and fish. Bright, not black.

Lighting: Summer sun with colorful shadows, and a separate character key light so that nothing sinks into shade.

Effects: Bold drawn anime FX on twos and threes. Sharp lightning with a white core, plasma trails, sheets of water pouring off the body, plumes, spray and a wall of water with real mass. Never particle mush or cotton-wool clouds.

Animation: Authentic hand-drawn anime timing, with characters on twos, strong key poses, natural holds, and overlapping movement. Huge things move slowly and heavily. Nothing clips, slides or floats.

Sound: An original epic score with ominous drones, brass and choir, near silence before the impact, then a colossal hit. Add a recurring whale-song motif, bow creak, charge whine, sonic boom, thunder and the sea, muffled underwater, all timed to the picture.
Direction: Cinematic shots, macro close-ups against huge wide shots, thoughtful staging, and pacing that builds from quiet tension to a devastating climax.

IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE

- 3D: No plastic materials, CGI shading, visible polygons, game-engine lighting, or computer-perfect perspective.
- Blocky "Minecraft" shapes: No plain boxes, empty flat surfaces, or toy-like proportions. Every surface carries design detail.
- SVG or vector art: No simple geometric shapes, perfect curves, uniform outlines, flat corporate illustration, or basic gradients.
- Web animation: No sliding layers, constant bobbing, floating parts, smooth software easing, or puppet-like joint rotation.
- Pasted-on elements: No 2D sprites floating in a 3D scene.
- AI art: No warped shapes, melted details, flickering, or changing designs.
- Non-anime art: No Western cartoon designs, realistic rendering, soft painterly shading on the characters, or generic digital illustration.
- Amateur work: No stiff poses, empty backgrounds, muddy colors, clip art, placeholders, or unfinished details.

You are free to change any part of the prompt, if it would result in better results.

The result should feel enormous, terrifying and beautiful, a blockbuster in bright anime colors.

Before finishing, inspect random frames as still images. If any frame does not look completely like real 2D anime, keep improving it.

Do not stop until every frame could pass as a still from a theatrical anime film.

2116606788241969445.prompt:
Build a 2D animated cutaway of a 9-cylinder radial aircraft engine called "RADIAL NINE" — a clean technical loop that shows how nine pistons share one crankshaft.
STYLE (strict)
Flat 2D technical front view on a deep navy background (#0b1220 or similar), like a premium engineering explainer.
Clean shapes with soft shading, thin light outlines, a subtle hatched pattern on cut metal walls.
Palette: light steel-grey metal; fresh fuel-air mixture in blue; combustion in orange to white; exhaust in smoky grey.
One square composition (1:1), the engine centred and filling ~80% of the square.
NO on-screen UI, no title, no labels by default. The only text is small cylinder numbers 1–9 engraved on the cylinder heads as part of the drawing.
THE ENGINE (must be mechanically correct)
Front view, with the propeller drawn as a faint translucent blur so the engine behind it stays visible.
Nine finned cylinders spaced evenly every 40° around a round crankcase, each cut open to show its piston.
Every cylinder head has an intake and an exhaust valve with rocker arms and pushrods.
A single-throw crankshaft in the centre. One master rod on cylinder 1 is attached directly to the crank pin; the other eight articulated link rods attach to pins on the master rod's big end, not to the crankshaft.
Because of the articulated rods, the pistons' motion is slightly non-uniform. Model the real linkage geometry rather than faking it with identical sine motion.
Four-stroke cycle: each cylinder fires once every two crankshaft revolutions.
Firing order 1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8, so the flashes jump around the ring skipping every other cylinder.
THE CYCLE (driven by one crank angle, all motion synchronized)
Intake: the intake valve opens and blue mixture flows in as the piston moves inward.
Compression: both valves closed, the mixture compresses and brightens.
Power: a spark and an orange flame front fill the cylinder and push the piston inward.
Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens and grey exhaust leaves through the exhaust stub.
Rockers and pushrods move in time with their valves.
Gases never pass through solid walls.
ANIMATION (starts on load)
Seamless loop of ~10–12 s at a readable speed (about one crankshaft revolution every 1.5 s), so the firing pattern reads as a spiral of flashes.
A brief 0.5× slow-down once per loop so the articulated rods can be followed.
Subtle heat glow on each cylinder head after it fires, slight engine vibration, the propeller blur spinning in sync with the crankshaft.
KEYBOARD (optional, nothing visible on screen)
Space pauses, S toggles slow motion, L toggles small labels (master rod, link rod, crank pin, intake, exhaust, spark plug), arrow keys change speed.
TECHNICAL
Canvas or SVG, any libraries you like (loaded from a CDN).
Everything works by opening index.html directly in the browser: no build step, no local server.
Starts automatically on load, no Start button. Smooth 60 fps.
The square stays centred and as large as possible at any window size, including phones.
Original content only.
When finished, open the page, check the firing order (1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8, each cylinder once per two revolutions), the articulated rod geometry, the loop and the browser console for errors, and fix any issues. Reply briefly with what was done and where the files are.

2103099194693271874.prompt:
[Y]ou are the director, animator, rigger, compositor, sound designer and render engineer for a 45–50 second animated short made entirely in code. The bar is "this looks like a real studio short and goes viral on X." Treat this as a multi-session production. Do not rush to a final render. Work in milestones, render stills constantly, look at them, criticize them honestly, and fix them.

0. The film in one line

Pip, a tiny, curious scrap-built robot, is happily rolling through his world when it starts regenerating around him. He slowly realizes someone is prompting his reality. The prompts get more absurd, he finally climbs onto the floating prompt box and types "let me out", and the camera pulls back to reveal his whole universe is a video playing on a phone propped up on a cluttered workbench, being watched by another Pip, who is about to get prompted too. Perfect loop.

The joke must land with zero dialogue. Pip communicates only through his eyes, antenna, body language and little robot chirps. Every 3–5 seconds there must be a new visual payoff.

1. The character (non-negotiable)

Study ./reference/pip_sheet.png carefully before writing any code. Open it, describe it back to yourself in detail, and write your findings into docs/character_bible.md:

Size: about 28 cm tall. He is small. The whole film should feel his scale.
Head: a wide, rounded-rectangle helmet in cream with a soft-yellow rim band framing a black glossy visor screen. His eyes live on that screen: two large glowing warm-cream eyes with dark pupils and a bright highlight. Small graphite ear-caps on each side. Wear, scratches and dusty-brown dirt around the edges.
Antenna: a thin graphite stalk on the top-right of the head with a small muted-orange signal flag. It is his "tail": it perks, droops, wiggles and vibrates with emotion.
Body: a boxy cream torso with yellow trim, warning-triangle decals, rivets and grime. A small chest compartment with a hatch that opens to show a tiny green sprout glowing softly. Back: panels, a vent grille, an orange panel, a small leaf decal.
Side decal: "PIP" lettering with orange diagonal stripes.
Arms: thin segmented graphite arms with yellow joint sleeves and three-finger claw grips. Very expressive.
Wheels: four chunky rubber wheels with yellow hubs and independent suspension, rugged and compact.
Personality: curious, kind, scrappy, expressive, always exploring. "Small bot, big feelings." He is never mean, even when furious; his anger is cute and determined.
Extract the exact palette from the sheet's swatches (sample the image with Python/PIL) into src/theme/palette.ts: Cream (body), Soft Yellow (primary), Muted Orange (accents), Graphite (metal/tech), Dusty Brown (wear & dirt), Mint Blue (lights/UI).

Identity lock rule: in every world, his helmet-and-visor silhouette, antenna flag, yellow trim, claw arms and four wheels must stay instantly recognizable. Worlds change his rendering style, never his design. The only intentional design change is the "more adorable" gag in Act 3, and even there his helmet shape, antenna and wheels stay.

2. Technical stack
Remotion (React + TypeScript) for frame-accurate, deterministic rendering. Output 1920×1080, 30 fps, H.264, high bitrate (CRF ~14). Landscape.
SVG for the character rig and most artwork. Canvas/WebGL (via @remotion/three or raw canvas) only where needed for particles, water, explosions, glow and noise effects.
SVG filters (feTurbulence, feDisplacementMap, feMorphology, feGaussianBlur) and custom canvas shaders for style "materials," scratches and grime.
@remotion/motion-blur (or your own sub-frame accumulation) for motion blur on fast action.
Python (numpy/scipy/PIL) for palette extraction, procedural audio synthesis and QA contact sheets. ffmpeg for muxing, loop checks and contact sheets.
Everything seeded and deterministic. No Math.random() without a seed.
No external copyrighted assets, no real brand logos or product names anywhere. The prompt box UI must be a generic, original design. Fonts only from Google Fonts (e.g., Inter for UI text, a rounded hand-lettered font for any handwritten notes).
Target hardware: MacBook Pro M4, 24 GB RAM. Keep render concurrency sensible.
3. The character rig (build this first, it's the whole film)

Build src/character/ as a proper 2D cutout rig:

Hierarchy: root → chassis (with suspension) → torso → neck joint → head (helmet + visor + ear-caps) → antenna → flag. Torso → shoulder → upper arm → forearm → claw (with swappable claw poses: open, closed, pinch-holding, pointing, poking/typing, gripping an edge, waving). Chassis → four wheels, each with its own suspension spring and rotation driven by distance travelled.
The visor face system (most important part): the eyes are shapes drawn on the black screen, so treat them as a fully procedural face. Parameters for eye size, roundness, top-lid cut, bottom-lid cut, pupil size and position, highlight position, glow intensity, squash/stretch, and special shapes (sparkle stars, happy arcs ^ ^, flat unimpressed lines, spirals, tiny hearts). Add a faint scanline and screen reflection over the eyes so it reads as a screen. Blink by squashing eyes vertically in 3–4 frames.
Expression targets: match the six on the sheet exactly: curious (with the "?" pop), shy (eyes low, looking away, blush marks), excited (happy arcs with little burst lines), worried (small eyes, sweat droplet), determined (angled top-lid cut), delighted (star sparkles with a heart pop). Also add: deadpan-to-camera (flat half-lidded eyes, antenna limp), horrified (tiny shaking pupils, eyes wide), furious-but-cute (determined + screen glow flickers orange), and three "glow-up" stages (see Act 3).
Secondary motion: antenna and flag on damped springs (this is his main expressive tool, use it constantly), suspension bounce on every stop and bump, arm sway, a tiny head lag when the body accelerates or brakes, dust puffs from wheels.
Turnaround: front, 3/4, side, back views matching the sheet, with clean view switching for turns.
Cycles: rolling forward (with speed lines and dust puffs as on the sheet), idle hum (gentle suspension breathing + occasional antenna twitch + blinks), recoil-in-fear, looking-up-in-wonder, holding a tiny object, reaching up, climbing, poke-typing.
Chest hatch: animatable open/close, with the sprout's soft green glow spilling out.
Style skin interface: the rig takes a style prop that changes line weight, fill treatment, texture, grime, outline boil, shading model and filters without changing geometry. This is how he stays himself across worlds.
Milestone 1 gate: render a "lineup" still: Pip in all four turnaround views + all six expressions, placed next to the reference sheet. Compare side by side. Iterate until someone who saw the sheet would say "that's Pip." Do not move on until this passes.
4. The worlds (style materials)

Each world is a full environment component with foreground, midground, background parallax layers and its own style skin for Pip. Build a shared WorldLayer system so all worlds share camera and depth logic.

Scale rule: the camera lives low, near Pip's eye level (about 20 cm off the ground). Everything is huge. People appear as giant legs and shoes, a curb is a cliff, a puddle is a lake. This is what makes a small robot cinematic.

Base world: golden-hour overgrown city. Match the header illustration of the sheet: warm sunset light, weathered stone and brick, moss and little plants, hazy tall buildings in the distance. Painterly, cozy, lived-in. This is "real life." Also used for the reveal.

Anime Tokyo. Crisp cel shading, bold outlines, glowing signs with invented (non-brand) shop names, speed lines, cherry petals drifting past him like giant pink snowflakes. His visor gets anime sparkle highlights.

Clay village. Soft rounded shapes, fingerprint/smudge noise texture, stop-motion stepping (render him "on twos"), warm tungsten lighting. He looks sculpted in plasticine.
Medieval battlefield. Muddy field, banners, distant catapults, smoke. Armored boots thunder past him. He rolls calmly between them, antenna ducking.
Toy-brick city. Everything built from generic stud-topped plastic bricks (no real brand styling or logos), glossy plastic highlights. Pip rendered with plastic sheen and slightly blockier wheels.
Underwater. Seabed street with coral lampposts, fish swimming past his visor, caustic light patterns, bubbles from his vents, his antenna flag waving slowly like seaweed.
Pencil sketch. Paper texture, graphite hatching, construction lines, eraser smudges, his lines boiling as if being redrawn every frame (match the sketch vignettes at the bottom of the sheet).
Running gag: the sprout. Pip starts the film carefully holding his tiny green sprout in one claw (the "holding a tiny object" pose). It survives every world and transforms with it: cel-shaded anime sprout with sparkles, clay sprout, sprout in a tiny battered helmet-pot, brick-built sprout, sprout releasing a bubble underwater, sketched sprout. He protects it every time the world changes. It is the emotional anchor of the film.
5. The signature transition: "regeneration"

World changes must look like an AI image re-generating, not like normal wipes. Build RegenTransition:

The frame breaks into drifting diffusion-style noise from the edges inward (not over his body at first), holds a few frames of structured noise, then the new world denoises in from coarse blobs to fine detail.

Pip's body lags one beat behind the world, briefly showing half-old / half-new style, then snaps to the new style skin. His visor glitches for 2 frames (scanline tear) during the snap. This half-state is the visual proof that he persists.

Subtle audio "whoosh-crackle" per regen, plus a tiny startled chirp from Pip on some of them.
Duration 8–12 frames each. Vary the direction and noise seed so it never feels repetitive.
6. Beat sheet (≈48 seconds at 30 fps)
Timing is a guide; adjust if a beat reads better slightly longer. The first 2 seconds must hook.
ACT 1: A GOOD MORNING (0:00–0:03)

Low tracking shot, base world. Pip rolls left-to-right along a mossy ledge, holding his sprout, eyes curious, antenna bobbing. Start mid-roll (needed for the loop).

At 0:02 the first regen hits without warning.

ACT 2: THE CASCADE (0:03–0:14)
Rapid world changes, about 1.4 s each: Anime Tokyo → Clay village → Medieval battlefield → Toy-brick city → Underwater → Pencil sketch.

Emotional progression: delighted at first (star eyes, he thinks it's wonderful), then curious ("?" pops), then worried (sweat drop, antenna droops), then he brakes hard in the sketch world with a suspension bounce and a skid mark.

Camera stays on a locked tracking framing so the only thing changing is the world, which makes the joke readable.
ACT 3: THE PROMPTS (0:14–0:30)
Base world returns. Pip looks up in wonder (pose from the sheet). In the sky, a giant floating prompt box fades in, glowing mint blue, glassy and rounded, with a soft original UI. Text types itself with a blinking cursor: "make it more cinematic" → enter key click sound.Letterbox bars slam in, the sun becomes absurd: enormous anamorphic lens flares, god rays, orange-and-teal grade, slow-motion dust, a single dramatic leaf drifting past his visor. His eyes squint into the flare. His antenna flag flaps heroically in wind he didn't ask for.

"add explosions"Huge cartoon-orange explosions bloom behind him in sequence with debris chunks. He does not turn around. His eyes go flat and half-lidded. He slowly rotates his head to look straight into the camera. Deadpan. Hold 1 full second. Then an explosion lands close and he snaps into the "recoiling in fear" pose from the sheet, the "!!" popping above him, shielding the sprout with his body.

"make the protagonist more adorable"Glow-up stage 1: his eyes grow bigger and shinier, blush marks appear, a tiny bow sprouts on his antenna. He sees his reflection in a puddle and his eyes turn horrified.

"more.": Stage 2: pastel repaint, eyes take over the whole visor with triple highlights, floating hearts and sparkles, his wheels become fluffy.
"MORE." (bigger font, screen shake): Stage 3: comically maximum cute. Plushie fur texture over his whole body, giant anime eyes, rainbow halo, a choir "aah" sting, heart confetti. His helmet shape, antenna and wheels stay so he's still clearly Pip. His eyes are still tiny and horrified inside the giant cute eyes, which is the joke.
ACT 4: HE SNAPS (0:30–0:38)
Pip vibrates, then the cute stages shatter off him like glass. He's back to normal, scuffed and furious (determined expression, screen flickering orange).
He opens his chest hatch and gently tucks the sprout inside for safety. Hatch closes with a click. This is the one quiet, kind beat in the chaos and it matters.
He races forward, launches off a rock, grabs the edge of the floating prompt box with both claws and hauls himself up, wheels spinning against the edge (match the "reaching toward a floating prompt box" pose). The camera tilts up with him.
On top of the box he holds backspace with one claw; the old prompt deletes letter by letter with fast clicks, and his visor reflects the vanishing text.

He poke-types with one claw, slowly and deliberately: "let me out". Winds up and smashes enter.

ACT 5: FREEZE AND REVEAL (0:38–0:47)
Everything freezes: debris mid-air, confetti mid-fall, dust suspended, Pip mid-pose on the box. All audio cuts to total silence for about 1 second.
Camera begins a smooth pull-back. The frame's edges reveal a rounded rectangle: his universe is a video on a phone screen. Keep pulling back: the phone is propped against a chipped mug on a cluttered workbench full of spare parts, wires, screws and scraps ("built from tomorrow's leftovers"). Sitting in front of it, tiny next to the giant phone, is another Pip, same scuffs, same antenna, watching.
The second Pip's eyes blink slowly. His antenna droops a little. A small quiet chirp.
ACT 6: THE LOOP (0:47–0:50)

Above the second Pip's head, the same mint-blue prompt box fades in and types: "make it more cinematic."

His eyes slowly slide upward toward it. His antenna flag goes stiff. On the enter key sound, hard cut to frame 1 of the film.
Loop engineering: the final shot's framing, lighting, and the start of a regen flicker must make the cut back to frame 1 feel intentional. The music must loop seamlessly across the cut. Verify by concatenating the video with itself (ffmpeg) and watching the seam.
7. Camera and cinematography

Virtual camera system: position, zoom, rotation, handheld micro-shake (seeded noise), shake impulses for explosions, tilt for the climb, dolly pull-back for the reveal.

Low camera height by default to sell his scale. Shallow depth-of-field feel: blurred foreground grass/pebbles and soft background, like a macro lens.
Depth: minimum 4 parallax layers per world. Atmospheric perspective (haze, desaturation with distance).
Motion blur on fast moves, debris, the jump and the climb.
Lighting per world: key/fill/rim implemented as gradient overlays and multiplied shadow layers on the rig. The visor glow should cast a faint warm light on nearby surfaces and on his own claws. Rim light on his helmet in every world.
Film finish pass on the whole frame: subtle grain, gentle vignette, very slight chromatic aberration only in the "cinematic" beat.
Composition: keep him on a clear third. His eyes must be readable at phone size, since most people will watch this on a phone.
8. Text and typography
Sky prompts: clean UI font, lowercase, typed at a natural human rhythm (not constant speed; tiny pauses, one small typo-and-backspace somewhere for realism).
The text must be readable in under a second on a phone. Test at 360 px wide.
No subtitles, no titles. The film opens cold.
9. Sound (procedural, original)
Create all audio in code (Python synthesis or offline Web Audio) and mix with ffmpeg:
Pip's voice: original synthesized chirps, boops and warbles built from sine/FM tones with pitch bends. Design a small emotional vocabulary: curious rising chirp, happy trill, worried wobble, startled squeak, grumpy low buzz, tiny sigh. He never speaks words.
Pip's body: servo whirs matched to arm and head moves, wheel crunch on gravel/stone, suspension creaks, hatch click, soft electrical hum on idle.
Score: a light, loopable, warm score whose instrumentation changes per world (koto/synth for anime, wooden marimba for clay, drums/horn for medieval, plastic clicks for bricks, muffled underwater filter, pencil scratch rhythm for sketch).
SFX: regen whoosh-crackle, keyboard typing clicks, enter "thunk", explosions with low-end, choir "aah" sting, glass shatter, total silence at the freeze, then quiet workshop ambience (a ticking clock, distant hum) in the reveal.

Loudness normalized to about −14 LUFS. Put stems in audio/stems/ so they can be swapped for a licensed track later.

10. Production workflow and self-improvement loop
Work in this order and don't skip gates:
Plan: write docs/character_bible.md, docs/shotlist.md (every shot with frame ranges, camera, expression, antenna state, world, SFX) and docs/style_guide.md. Show me the shot list before building.
Rig: build Pip, pass the lineup gate (section 3).
Worlds: build each world as a standalone still with Pip in it. Render all 7 as a single contact sheet. Check the identity lock and the scale feel.
Transitions: build RegenTransition, render a 5-second test.

Animatic: assemble the whole film at 960×540 with rough motion and placeholder audio. Watch it. Fix pacing first.

Full animation pass, then polish pass (secondary motion, easing, timing, antenna acting), then finish pass (lighting, grain, blur, grime).
Audio pass and mix.
Final render.
For every shot, run this critique loop at least 3 times:
Render 3–5 stills at key frames with npx remotion still, open them and look at them properly.
Score each 1–10 on: Pip matches the reference, emotion reads instantly from eyes + antenna, joke is clear without sound, composition, sense of scale, depth, lighting, polish, readability at phone size.
Write the scores and the three biggest problems into docs/review_log.md, fix them, re-render, re-score. Continue until every category is at least 8, then move on.
After each full preview render, make an ffmpeg contact sheet (one frame every 0.5 s) and review the whole film's flow in one image.

Be honest in reviews. If something looks cheap, say it and fix it. Usual failures to hunt for: stiff or dead antenna, wheels sliding instead of rolling, eyes that feel like stickers instead of a glowing screen, missing suspension weight, identical-looking transitions, muddy text, and off-model proportions.

11. Deliverables
out/pip_final_1080p.mp4: the film.
out/pip_loop_check.mp4: the film played twice back to back, to prove the loop.
out/poster_frame.png: the best single frame for the X post thumbnail (probably Pip deadpanning at camera with explosions behind him).

out/lineup.png: Pip across all worlds.

Clean, commented source with a README explaining how to re-render.
Start with step 1. Ask me anything essential before building, otherwise make strong creative decisions yourself.

架空の海賊船（17世紀のガレオン船風・3本マスト・船名なし）について、
CAD図面と Blender 動画を作ってください。

【図面】2D の DXF のみ（3Dモデルの書き出しは不要）。単位 mm、A2 の図枠と表題欄つき。
1. 甲板平面図 S=1:100（船の中心線を y=0 にした実際の位置で描く）
2. 側面図（帆装図）S=1:150
3. 正面図・船尾図・中央横断面図 S=1:150
特記事項に「架空の船のイメージで、実在の船の図面ではない」と書く。
寸法は Python の形状モジュール1つで決め、図面と動画の両方がそれを読み込む。

【動画】Blender（EEVEE）、1920×1080・24fps・本編20秒＋ロゴ3.5秒、音つき MP4。
1. 羊皮紙の巻物が広がり、セピアのインクで描いた甲板平面図が現れる
（方位盤・題字・赤い封蝋つき、真上から）
2. 図面の線が光るワイヤーとして立ち上がる
3. 竜骨 → 肋材 → 外板（下から1段ずつ）→ 甲板 → 大砲 → マスト → 帆桁 → 索具 → 帆
→ 金の飾り・角灯・ドクロ旗 の順に組み上がる（カメラは船に寄る）

- 図面のプレビュー画像を目で見て、文字の重なりを直す
- 本番の前にテスト静止画を数枚描いて確認する
- 本番レンダーは軽い設定で、PC を休ませながら回す。始める前に所要時間を伝えて了承を取る

2105315982525014067.prompt:
TITLE: "SPARK"

An around 15-second 3D animated shot in the painterly style of the show Arcane (Fortiche).

Made in Blender, or any other tool if superior. Widescreen, no dialogue.

GOAL

The top priority is replicating Arcane's visual and animation style as perfectly as possible, in every way. Someone watching should believe it came from the same studio.

Take as much time and effort as needed. Replicate the technique and look perfectly. Spend as much time as needed, ensuring it's perfect in every way.

SCENE (loose — adapt freely)

A small mechanical creature (not humanoid), something like a brass-and-crystal moth, wakes up on a cluttered inventor's workbench at night. Its crystal core ignites with glowing energy, and it bursts into the air in a swirl of sparks. Change the details, framing, or action if something else shows off the style better. You can animate something else completely different if you want—anything you pick, whatever you can do best—that will also look identical to Arcane.

PROCESS

1. RESEARCH: Before building anything, study Arcane's style in depth. Find references and breakdowns of Fortiche's technique (interviews, making-of material, artist breakdowns). Write down every defining element: textures, shading, line work, color, lighting, frame rate, effects, camera, compositing.

2. STYLE GUIDE: Turn that into a written checklist and a small style frame (a single still image) before animating. Compare it side by side with reference stills and revise until it matches.

3. BUILD: Model, texture, light, and animate following the checklist.

4. REVIEW: Compare frames against Arcane references repeatedly. List every difference you can see and fix it. Repeat until no noticeable differences remain.

STYLE ELEMENTS TO MATCH (at minimum)

- Hand-painted textures with visible brushstrokes on every surface; nothing looks procedural or photographic.

- Stylized, painterly shading with designed light/shadow shapes, not realistic falloff.

- Animation on 2s for characters/objects, with strong poses, snappy timing, anticipation, and smear frames; camera moves smooth on 1s.

- Hand-drawn 2D effects (sparks, energy, smoke, glints, glow) layered over the 3D, animated on 2s with graphic shape language.

- Bold, moody color: warm light vs. saturated glowing accents, rich colored shadows, strong rim light, bloom.

- Painterly compositing: brush-like filtering, grain, subtle texture over the image.

- Cinematic camera: shallow depth of field, purposeful movement, weight on impacts.

SOUND

Detailed, cinematic sound design that matches the action and mood.

Make everything as good as possible: animation, models, textures, effects, lighting, and sound. Use any tools or programs needed. You may study references online and imitate techniques, and copy things, but do not directly use assets you did not create. Keep the whole shot in one consistent style so the 3D, painted textures, and 2D effects feel like a single hand-crafted image.

Do not use memory or previous chats.

You can use any other tools, programs, plugins, literally anything. Use anything at your disposal.

You can use different processes than outlined in this, or animate something else than described, but it should absolutely look as close as possible to the TV show Arcane. Make it perfect in every way and identical.

2103299766473875778.prompt:
INFINIZOOM

Build infinizoom: a procedural infinite-zoom world. The deliverable is a
self-contained BunJS project. Running `bun run server` must build and serve it
(wire up the corresponding "server" script in package.json). Three local assets
exist in this directory and must be used: ./macbook_interior.png (a real MacBook
Pro teardown photo), ./apple_m4_scheme.png (Apple's M4 die floorplan diagram),
and ./wallpaper.jpg (a 1920×1200 desktop wallpaper photo). Load the wallpaper
from this local file — never fetch content from external servers (the sole
exception: three.js itself may be imported from a CDN by URL).

The world

A single 3D world is traveled indefinitely along a fixed camera track that zooms
through these levels:

Main route: a room → a desk → a MacBook Pro → inside the chassis → the logic
board → the Apple M4 package → the M4 die → a performance core → an integer ALU
block → a standard logic cell → a FinFET transistor → a material cross-section
inside the fin → the silicon crystal lattice → one unit cell → an atom → its
nucleus → a nucleon → a quark. Logic gates and circuits (AND, OR, etc.) should
be animated as it computes.

Screen branch: exactly one bifurcation, hovering above the MacBook. Choosing the
other side dives into the display instead: the screen → the display panel →
pixel tiles → a pixel block → one pixel → its R/G/B sub-pixel LEDs → the
emissive layer → an emitter molecule → and converges to the same atom → nucleus
→ nucleon → quark tail. The leds must be accurate: 1-to-1 mapping from screen
pixels to leds, and their colors must match the color of that pixel. The screen
is animated and the LEDs are updated to match the animation in real time.

Riding the track forward IS zooming in; riding backward is zooming out. The
design must extend additively: adding a new structure = one render function +
one call in its parent; adding a bifurcation = one more route; a future backward
extension (t < 0: out the window → city → planet → universe) must require only
prepending track levels. A time parameter must be threaded through everything so
all animation stays possible at any depth.

Architecture (hard constraints)

- Mutable state is EXACTLY: one float t (position along the track), one branch
  bitstring (0 = left/A, 1 = right/D; a bit is pushed when passing a fork and
  popped when backing out below it), and raw input (keys held, mouse position).
  Every frame is a pure function of (t, branches, raw input, wall-clock time).
  No other state — no scene graph, no node objects, no stored world data, no
  caches of world structure.
- Renderers are pure functions that call their children directly: render_room()
  calls render_desk() calls render_macbook() … down to render_quark(). No
  dispatch layer, no classes. The call stack is the scene traversal.
- Scale-space warping via local unit frames: floats cannot hold meters and
  femtometers at once, so every renderer works in its own ~unit-sized local
  frame, and the camera is re-expressed into each child frame. Geometry math is
  done camera-relative in doubles, cast to float only at the very end, so the
  picture is artifact-free across all ~17 decades of scale. The exact same
  layout constants must place structures for rendering AND author the track —
  one source of truth, or the camera drifts visibly off the line.
- Immediate-mode rendering over three.js: every frame, the recursion emits
  primitives into instanced pools; three.js is only a rasterizer. Nothing
  off-screen or sub-pixel is emitted or recursed into.

The track and the camera

- Speed: fast. The whole main ride should take roughly 20 seconds, with a
  comfortable, constant-feeling time per level (exponential zoom feel) and
  gentle easing near the fork and the track ends.
- Shape: gently curved arcs. Not wandering, roundabout, or random-direction —
  but also NOT dead-straight rays. Soft, purposeful curves.
- The green line: the track is always visible in-scene as a translucent green
  line. It must be an infinitesimal line: ~2 pixels wide on screen at EVERY
  distance, implemented as a true GL line primitive (not tubes, not rods, not
  meshes of any kind), transparent (never rock-solid), and it must NEVER grow
  wider as it approaches or passes the camera — it is literally a path line,
  visible both near and far.
- The camera must never look at nothing. At every instant of the ride the view
  must be filled with structure. Concretely: every level approach is a diagonal
  glide (roughly 45°) over the parent surface — never a low horizontal skim
  (which puts empty void in the upper half of the screen) and never a
  straight-down drop (which degenerates the camera roll). Every level must
  render rich, non-uniform content at the distance where the camera arrives —
  never a flat gray plate.
- Dive points land dead-center inside meaningful sub-structures. The line must
  enter the CENTER of one of the small colored squares (a specific core on the
  die, a specific block in the core, a specific pixel on the screen) — never a
  border, edge, gap, seam, or gray filler zone. The boundary transitions between
  levels (e.g. performance core → integer ALU block, "100 µm across") must be
  scrutinized: the camera must be looking at detailed structure the whole way
  through.
- Occlusion never pops: every shell the camera is about to pierce (the keyboard
  deck, the transistor's gate, the LED's cathode, the screen's cover glass…)
  fades away smoothly as a pure function of t shortly before the camera reaches
  it, and fades back identically when riding out.

Controls and HUD

- W rides deeper, S rides back.
- At the bifurcation: a big translucent ‹ on the left edge and › on the right
  edge of the screen, each labeled with its key (A / D), with the currently
  selected side highlighted/glowing. No sentence-style instruction text.
- Mouse moves the glance direction with a full 360° range — the rider can look
  all the way around, including behind.
- A title at the top-left always names where we are right now (e.g. "performance
  core") together with the current physical scale ("3.2 mm across").

Content — fidelity and density

Everything must be densely detailed — think "10× more detail than feels
sufficient" — and hiding must be un-aggressive: distant and peripheral objects
stay visible; more detail is always preferred over less. Everything plausible
must be animated and alive.

- The room and desk: a believable day-lit room (window, curtains, floor, walls,
  shelf, chair, door, rug, a wall clock whose hands actually run, lamps, cables)
  and a believable desk (the MacBook, a potted plant, paper, a mug, books,
  phone, pens…).
- The MacBook exterior: correct proportions, full keyboard with per-key legends,
  trackpad, ports, hinge, screen bezel with notch and camera.
- The MacBook interior: there are many components inside a MacBook — reproduce
  them in pixel-perfect locations matching ./macbook_interior.png: the two fans
  (with visibly SPINNING, clearly readable impeller blades — use few chunky
  blades, not a dense blur), the S-curved heat pipe and heat spreader, the black
  logic board carpeted in passives with EMI shields and chips, the antenna bar
  along the hinge, side port boards, the 4-corner + 2-tall-center battery cell
  layout with printed labels, aluminum struts, the trackpad flex cable running
  down the middle to its gold connector, the flanking speakers, tape, thermal
  pads, screws — all of it.
- The M4 die: block placement faithful to ./apple_m4_scheme.png (4 P-cores +
  shared L2, 6 E-cores + L2, 10 GPU cores, 16 Neural Engine cores, SLC,
  media/display engines, ISP, Secure Enclave, memory PHYs on the edges), with no
  bare/gray substrate anywhere — every area is a labeled block, and blocks show
  interior sub-structure at every intermediate zoom. The CPU interior (core
  floorplan: caches, decoders, schedulers, ALUs, FP units, register files…) must
  be greatly detailed, not a few flat rectangles.
- Digital circuits doing operations — explicitly a top-priority feature: the
  zoom must pass through logic that is visibly COMPUTING. Standard cells are
  real gates (AND/OR/NAND/NOR/XOR/NOT): their input nets carry live 0/1 signals
  (bright = 1, dark = 0), their output is the actual boolean function of the
  inputs, pulses race along wires when gates switch, and whole logic blocks
  twinkle with switching activity at every zoom level.
- Animated electronic simulation: the FinFET's gate runs a live drive waveform,
  and while it is open, charge carriers visibly flow from source to drain.
  Continue through real materials: gate oxide, dopants, the diamond-cubic
  silicon lattice at its true 0.543 nm pitch, into atoms with orbiting
  electrons, a nucleus with protons/neutrons and an animated gluon field, down
  to quarks.
- The screen must be REAL: a real image at real MacBook-panel fidelity — the
  bundled ./wallpaper.jpg photo as the desktop background, with a procedurally
  drawn OS on top (menu bar, dock with recognizable icons, overlapping
  application windows: a code editor with syntax-colored lines, a file browser,
  a terminal with a blinking cursor, and a video window that visibly plays,
  animating at full frame rate). Never a mosaic of colored squares. All levels
  of the screen (full panel → tiles → pixels → sub-pixel brightness) must sample
  the SAME image function so content never changes across zoom, and detail must
  increase strictly monotonically as the camera approaches — at no zoom distance
  may the screen become LESS detailed than it was a moment before.
- The sub-pixel LEDs: each LED is lit by the ACTUAL channel value of the
  on-screen image at that exact pixel — realistic and accurate, not default
  colors. Because the screen animates, the LEDs visibly CHANGE color over time.
  The dive targets a pixel inside the playing video, where R, G and B clearly
  differ from each other and keep changing. Inside, an LED is not a solid: model
  the full OLED stack — the TFT drive circuit with its data/scan lines and
  storage capacitor, the reflective anode, transport layers, the emission layer,
  the semi-transparent cathode, auxiliary wiring, spacers, encapsulation — with
  a live simulation: holes drift up, electrons drift down, they recombine in the
  emission layer with a flash, and photons fly up and out. Below that, the
  emissive layer resolves into a molecular film, then a single emitter molecule
  built of real atoms, joining the shared atomic tail.

Visual-quality laws

- Nothing ever pops, flickers, or z-fights — anywhere, at any scale, moving in
  either direction. In particular: never emit overlapping coplanar surfaces or
  nested coincident translucent volumes; and any material exempted from fog
  (emissive screens, glass, glow) must still be manually distance-faded and
  culled, or shells belonging to enclosing structures will haunt the camera at
  deep zooms as giant flickering planes.
- All LOD transitions are smooth morphs or strictly-finer refinements of
  identical content — never a swap to something coarser, blurrier, or
  differently colored.
- Spinning/periodic animations must be tuned to be perceptible (no temporal
  aliasing that freezes or scrambles them).
- Runs at 60 fps.

Code Quality

Ensure your implementation is concise, minimal, elegant. Use pure functions as
much as possible. Keep it very Haskell-like, even though it is TypeScript. Most
of the complexity of the function comes from the different objects that are
rendered, and each object is a render function. Each renderable object must live
in its own file at src/render/<name>.ts — that directory is the one that scales
as we add more renderables. Organize the project such that it can scale by just
adding more render functions/files under src/render/. Avoid unnecessary
complexity.

2115786060231770351.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my video idea (one line is fine), the setting, the length (60-90 s) and the narrator (an ElevenLabs voice, or "free" for a local text-to-speech). Everything is built in code: no AI images, no AI video. Make it MY story, not a copy of an example.
</inputs>

<format>
The style is a second-person survival thriller with stickmen, built as a series:
- "Imagine you…" hook with a time stamp in the first 3 s
- a HUD with the DAY number and a clock that moves forward through the episode
- 3-4 RULES, each one paid off on screen
- a threat that escalates and is mostly shown, not told
- a twist that makes one rule impossible
- a two-choice ending ("DO YOU OPEN IT?" style, a green and a red option, "COMMENT BELOW") and "FOLLOW FOR DAY 2"
Around 20-30 voice lines, 60-90 s, a new shot every 1.5-3 s.
</format>

<story>
Write a beat sheet and the script first and show me both before building anything.
- One line = one visual. Rules are short commands.
- Open a new question every ~10 s and only answer it with a bigger one.
- Put the viewer in POV for the scary parts: what you see through a door, a window, a phone, a peephole.
- The ending is a choice where both options look bad.
- Write numbers twice: the caption form ("11:58 PM") and the spoken form ("eleven fifty-eight P M") for the text-to-speech.
- Rotate settings between episodes (apartment, subway, school at night, hospital, cabin, plane, office, motel) and fit the threat to the setting.
</story>

<look>
Pick a palette per story, but keep the language:
- real 3D low-poly sets with real lights and shadows; the mood comes from light (one warm practical, one cold fill, one strong accent such as a door gap, a screen or a siren)
- the stickman is flat and 2D-looking: a light body with a thick dark outline, round strokes, dot eyes, no mouth; give the main character one mark (a scar, a cap, a colour) so doubles and callbacks read
- the overlay: a monospace HUD top-left, chunky captions (1-3 words, key words in an accent colour), a tilted rule sticker with a big condensed title, phone screens drawn in 2D
- banned: AI frames, glossy 3D characters, emojis, music with vocals, long captions
</look>

<shots>
A library to adapt to the story (never use all of them):
- the opener: a camera move that starts tight on you and pulls out to show where you are
- POV phone in your hands (2D phone UI, two stick thumbs)
- a macro on the one detail that matters
- outside chaos from above (balcony, bridge, window): physics vehicles, a running crowd, something collapsing or burning
- third-person action in the room: walking with planted feet, reaching, hesitating, barricading
- POV interaction: throwing, holding a torch, opening something
- a close-up of your face for the reaction
- a low angle on a door or vent: light leaking in, shadows moving
- knocks, shakes, things falling
- a fisheye peephole, camera or window view of the threat stepping closer
- the choice screen and the end card
</shots>

<tools>
What each tool is for. Install whatever is missing, and ask me before anything paid:
- three . js: the 3D engine; it runs inside a web page. Download its module file locally so renders don't depend on the internet. Use its post-processing passes for bloom, plus one custom lens shader for vignette, grain, fisheye and colour fringing.
- cannon-es: a JavaScript physics engine for vehicles, falling debris and collapses.
- Playwright (Python): opens the page in a real browser (Edge or Chrome with the GPU on) and captures every frame as an image.
- ffmpeg: the command-line video and audio tool. It joins the frames into an MP4, cuts and filters the audio (highpass, lowpass and echo for voices behind doors), mixes, normalises loudness and makes the phone-size copy.
- ElevenLabs, or Kokoro (free local text-to-speech), for the narrator.
- faster-whisper: free local speech-to-text with word timestamps. Use it to cut the voice cleanly and to time every caption.
- numpy and Pillow: to check audio levels and make contact sheets of stills.
- Sound: free downloaded sound effects from Mixkit (never synthesized) and a dark cinematic drone or tension bed with no vocals.
</tools>

<build>
1. One HTML page (film . html) with the 3D renderer at 1080x1920 drawn into a 2D canvas that also holds the overlay. A function window . seek (t) draws frame t and must be a pure function of time; every cut, sound and move is keyed to the word times.
2. Stickman. Draw each figure with 2D canvas strokes onto its own texture and put it on a plane that always faces the camera, with an alpha test so it casts a real shadow and slight emissive so it reads in the dark. Pose with joint angles, and walk with 2-bone IK so the planted foot never slides.
3. Physics and cloth. Simulate once at load with a fixed timestep, record the positions, then sample them by time, so every render is identical. Cloth (sheets, curtains, flags) is a verlet particle grid with wall and floor collisions and pinned points you can release.
4. Voice. If you generate one long take, never cut it at the API's character timestamps: they drift and slice words. Transcribe the take with faster-whisper word timestamps, match it to the script, cut only in real silence between lines, and only add pause where the natural one is too short.
5. Captions. Re-transcribe each final line, normalise numbers ("6:42" = "6 42", "AM" = "a m"), align the caption words to what was heard, and snap each word to its real start in the audio. Check that every caption has voice under it within ~120 ms.
6. Render. Playwright steps window . seek through every frame at 30 fps, and ffmpeg encodes a high-quality master, then a phone copy under 30 MB.
7. Mix with ffmpeg: the voice on top, the music about 12-14 dB under it, one sound effect per event, a dip before the big moment, loudness at -14 LUFS, then a scan for dropouts.
</build>

<gotchas>
- is narrow: a normal lens sees very little sideways, so use wider lenses indoors and keep the subject close to the aim point.
- Glass behind a solid frame is invisible: build mirrors and windows as a frame around a real hole.
- Dust spread everywhere reads as stars, so keep it inside light beams.
- Night shots go black after compression, so give each one a cold fill light.
- Fog swallows distant things.
- Never judge a reference or your own render from one frame every few seconds; check motion at the full frame rate.
- Check cuts, captions and audio joints with numbers before every full render.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the idea, show me the beat sheet and script, then 6 stills of the key shots before rendering the full video.
</start>

2117602113509294520.prompt:
Ask me for my topic (a what-if, a "why does X happen", a true story, or how something works), or pitch 3 with one shocking true angle each. Ask which image model I have (GPT Image 2, or another that takes reference images at 4K) and which voice service (ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free). Then write a 55-65 s script and a shot plan, and show me both before you spend anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1920x1080 flat vector explainer in the style of the big infographic animation channels. Every scene is a full illustrated place (a lab, a street, a classroom, a stage) with characters acting the line out.
Flat colour shapes, no outlines, one slightly darker flat shade for form, a muted palette (dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple), salmon-pink skin, big heads, dot eyes.
A new scene every 2-4 s and a hard cut on every sentence that changes the idea. A white splat wipe (0.2 s in, 0.2 s out) between big sections. The camera always drifts 2-4% or pans.
Text lives only on things in the world: signs on posts, hanging boards, chalkboards, building panels and screens.
- It is typed in Montserrat 800 at 26-34 letters a second. Each letter arrives 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right, then settles in 0.18 s.
- Ink is #2b2d42 on white boards.
- A red X (#d62828, 30 px round strokes, two strokes of 0.11 s each) goes over every wrong idea.
- Every date gets a white 330x120 card top left with an orange #f4a261 calendar.
- Headlines are white 92-96 px caps on a flat colour (#e2552f with drifting lighter puffs, or #5b3fa6 with slowly turning #6a4cb6 gears).
Banned: outlines, motion-design UI floating over the art (code editors, glass cards, checklists), emoji, burned-in subtitles, any channel's logo, a still frame longer than 1 s, and a character who doesn't move.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: the voice decides, 55-65 s at about 190 words per minute.
0 s a second-person hook that flips what the viewer assumes, acted out literally, then a red X on the denial line → 3-8 s the stakes in one shocking true line, with icons popping in one per word → 8-11 s the subject revealed under a spotlight, its name typed on a sign → 11-18 s the origin: the real place with its name typed on its own sign, a date card, people walking in or out of it → 18-24 s the types or parts, landing one by one on their names, each labelled → 24-25.5 s "so how does it work?" as a headline with question marks popping → 25.5-36 s the mechanism acted out in 2-3 places (a chalkboard, a machine, a map), with a counter rolling up to the big number → 36-46 s what it leads to, with characters who react (jump, turn, a "!" pops) → 46-55 s the twist that ties back to the hook → 55 s the last line is a question to the viewer, the viewer character from the hook reacts, and the sign holds to the end.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, librosa. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art: everything at 3840x2160, with 3-5 frames of the reference channel as style references (crop their logo off first).
- One EMPTY plate per scene: no people, straight-on, open floor, blank signs and screens to write on in code.
- Character sheets on solid chroma green #00B140, with nothing green on anyone.
- Draw any character who gestures a lot WITHOUT ARMS, only round shoulder sockets, so code draws the arms. Draw everyone else in the exact pose their scene needs: side view at a desk, side view walking, seen from behind, sitting.
3. Cutouts:
- The background is every pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40, within 110 of the median green, connected to the border.
- Add a 2 px soft alpha band, and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it.
- Split heads at the neck, drawing hands, and walkers' legs below the coat hem.
- Refill each hole with inpainting from the body's own colours (transparent pixels masked too), so a turning piece never shows a gap.
4. Voice:
- Pick it by measuring median pitch (pyin) and MFCC timbre against a clip of the narrator you want.
- Generate one take, cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, and atempo it to the target length.
- Get word timestamps with faster-whisper. Every cut, sign and gesture starts on a real word.
5. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window. seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
- Arms: two-bone IK tubes (upper 118, lower 112, 36 thick for a 918 px tall sprite) with mitten hands that open, point or make a fist.
- Faces blink for 0.14 s every 2.7-4.2 s. Heads nod ±0.035 rad. Drawing hands scribble ±8 px.
- Walks:
- Thighs swing ±0.42 rad, and the knee bends 0.75·cos² on the swing.
- The hips drop so the planted foot stays down.
- The body moves 1.5 leg lengths per cycle, so feet never slide.
- Draw each plate inside the same camera transform as everything on it, and clamp the camera to the plate's edges.
- Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a fade.
6. Render: Playwright Chromium with --allow-file-access-from-files, 60 fps, 6 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, ffmpeg libx264 at CRF 16. Before rendering, show me two 16-frame contact sheets and fix empty boards, overflowing text, covered faces and black edges.
7. Sound:
- Music: a light curious documentary bed (free on Pixabay), 10-11 dB under the voice in every phrase.
- SFX: Mixkit, placed by their peaks. A typewriter tick on typed signs, a whoosh on wipes and drops, a pop on signs and icons, a hit on the red X, a ding on ticks.
- Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
Some image models ignore "no arms"; GPT Image 2 follows it. On outline-free art a floating flood fill leaks into dark clothes, so key by border-connected green instead. Look up repeated words by their occurrence number (the third "and", the fourth "this"), or cuts land on the wrong line; scan the render for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut. When a scene has a screen or a sign, write on the plate's own blank one (measure its rectangle), never on a card floating over the art.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, or pitch 3, then show me the script and the shot plan.

2121982602122760352.prompt:
# OBJECT STROBE: a product film built entirely in code

> Paste this into Claude Code in an empty folder. Replace `[OBJECT]` once, in the line below. Nothing else needs editing.

**OBJECT = [OBJECT]**

You are the technical director and the art director on a 9.6-second vertical loop for Instagram Reels. The hero is
[OBJECT], modelled entirely in code, with no imported models, no stock assets, no logos and no brand names. The film reads as the
output of a machine-vision system diagnosing [OBJECT]:
- the object comes apart and is inspected part by part;
- it goes back together and is pushed past its limit;
- it recovers and settles into one clean hero frame that loops into frame 0 without a seam.

Under the analysis graphics, each part strobes between three passes: **solid** (finished material), **glass**
(dispersive x-ray), and **field** (a simulation plot of the one physical quantity that matters to [OBJECT]).

Work like a studio, not like a demo: every decision below has a reason, and every number on screen has to be true.

---

## 0. How you work

- Work only inside this folder. Keep scripts in `scripts/`, frames in `renders/`, finished files in `deliver/`, notes in `board/`.
- **Every frame is a pure function of its frame number.** No accumulated state and no randomness without a seed. Any frame
can be re-rendered alone and match its neighbours.
- **One GPU, one render.** Never run two Blender renders at once. Run anything longer than two minutes in the background.
- **Ask before installing software, downloading fonts or spending money.** Say what, from where and how big.
- **Show, then continue.** At each checkpoint (★), build a contact sheet and show it to me before going on:
- every 6th frame with frame numbers burned in;
- 100 % crops where detail matters.
- Write a `README.md` as you go: what each script does and the exact commands to reproduce the result.

## 1. Preflight

Check, report in one table, and fix what's missing (after asking):

| Need | Check | If missing |
|---|---|---|
| Blender ≥ 4.2 (needs the *Khronos PBR Neutral* view transform) | `blender --version`. On Windows also try `C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\*\blender.exe`; on macOS `/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender` | `winget install BlenderFoundation.Blender` / `brew install --cask blender` / the official .tar.xz from https://blender.org/ on Linux |
| GPU for Cycles | in Blender's Python: `cycles` prefs `get_devices()`; prefer OPTIX > CUDA > METAL > HIP | CPU works: halve the samples, render at 50 % first, and tell me the time estimate |
| ffmpeg | `ffmpeg -version` | winget `Gyan.FFmpeg` / brew `ffmpeg` / apt `ffmpeg` |
| Python 3.10+ with numpy, opencv-python, pillow | make a local `.venv`, install there, never globally | — |
| Fonts: **Fira Mono** (data) and **Space Grotesk** (tags), both SIL OFL from Google Fonts | look in system or user font folders | ask, then download into `fonts/` and load them by path |

Then render one 540×960 test frame of a cube with the final render settings. Report the device and seconds per frame,
and project the full render time before you build anything.

## 2. Study the object ★

Before modelling, write `board/OBJECT.md`:

1. **Anatomy.** List 25–50 real parts of [OBJECT] with their real names: housings, inner mechanism, fasteners, seals, the
small parts people never see. Give each one:
- a group (shell / core / small);
- a primary material;
- an **explode vector** (direction and distance along the object's natural assembly axis; large shells travel farthest).
2. **The field.** Pick the ONE physical quantity [OBJECT] truly lives with:
- heat for an engine part;
- load for a structure;
- pressure or flow for a valve or a lung;
- charge for a battery;
- vibration for a speaker.

Name it, give it a unit, a realistic working range and a **limit**. This becomes the story.
3. **The story in four beats**, specific to [OBJECT]:
- cold, at rest;
- working, the field rises in a front across the object, from source to far end;
- **over the limit**, the most extreme frame of the film;
- recovery, a front running back.
4. **Proportions.** Overall size, key diameters and thicknesses, from real-world references you know. Turn them into one
constants table that all geometry reads from.

## 3. Build ([OBJECT] in code)

- Model with signed distance functions in numpy and mesh them with surface nets plus a few Newton steps onto the surface
(crisp edges, no blobby marching-cubes look).
- Use smooth unions for cast parts, hard booleans for machined ones.
- Use real threads on fasteners.
- Use bpy only for assembly and materials.
- Each part is its own object. Each one stores custom properties: `xv` (explode vector), `grp`, `seed`, `tbase` (field
value 0–1) and `hamp` (field noise amplitude).
- Cache SDF results to disk. Decimate large shells to a sane vertex budget (≈ 3 M vertices total is fine).
- **Hero asset bar:** sculpt-level detail on the parts the camera dwells on. Detail density here buys more than more parts:
bevels, bosses, ribs, casting seams, machined faces. Do not show a primitive blockout as the hero.
- ★ Look-dev sheet: four configurations (assembled / exploded / core only / close-up) × three passes, rendered at 50 %.

## 4. Look

- **One `Strobe` shader node group** on every part, switched per object through Attribute nodes (OBJECT type): `st` 0 solid,
1 glass, 2 field.
- **Glass:** three Glass BSDFs on R, G and B at IOR ≈ 1.47 / 1.51 / 1.57, added together. This is cheap dispersion with
rainbow edges.
- **Field:** object-space 4D noise around `tbase`, plus a radial and an axial term, fed through one colour ramp. Emission
rises with the field value, so hot parts glow and cold ones read as a scan.
- **The field palette has two hues, never a rainbow:**
- cold: navy → cobalt → ice;
- an unlit dark band between them;
- hot: ember → red → orange → near-white.

No green and no yellow-green: they read as engineering software, not as a film. Define the ramp once (sRGB hex) and use
the same ramp in the shader, the legend and every inset. In the cold acts, damp the noise so the scan stays blue.
- Studio world: dark ground, two or three hard softboxes. Camera and transmission rays see a pale environment, so the glass
reads.
- **Film transparent.** Backdrops are composited later, which lets the backdrop change per act.
- Khronos PBR Neutral view transform, exposure −1, 16-bit RGBA PNG.

## 5. Timeline: 288 frames = 6 bars at 150 BPM

One beat is 12 frames and an eighth is 6. **Every cut lands on an eighth.** Act lengths:

| frames | act | configuration | what happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–11 | acquire | assembled, glass ghost, **light** backdrop | the hook: the most beautiful material on frame 0 |
| 12–53 | separation | explode flight | outer parts leave first, small inner parts follow; ease-out, no overshoot |
| 54–89 | inspection | exploded, slow drift | **one continuous shot** that keeps the flight's framing; only materials strobe |
| 90–131 | core lock | close-up on the heart part, outer shells hidden | strip light along the edges, f/1.4 depth of field, three field pulses on beats |
| 132–167 | reassembly | exact reverse order | inner parts seat first, shells close last; the camera follows the shells |
| 168–215 | working | assembled | the field front runs source → far end, on the same curve the graphics draw |
| 216–245 | **limit** | assembled | the extreme of the film: everything in the field pass, an alarm flicker on the beat (2.5 Hz) |
| 246–269 | recovery | assembled | a front runs back; parts return to the solid pass one by one |
| 270–287 | clean | assembled, solid, **light**, **no graphics** | the product alone; framing, drift and rotation run into frame 0 |

- Material states are random only in the diagnostic acts (blocks of 1–4 frames, seeded per part). In the story acts they
are **deterministic**: a part's pass follows the front.
- **Never intercut configurations that read as different assembly states.** Hold one configuration per act.
- Acts 168–269 are **one continuous camera move**: one slow push and orbit, with no cuts inside the story.

## 6. Camera and motion

- A fixed shot per configuration, with the object's main axis at about −27° on screen and a low, slightly heroic angle.
- **Auto-framing:** project a subsample of the real mesh vertices (not bounding boxes) and fit the lens to a fill target.
Re-aim at the visual centre, and compute it once per act so repeated shots match.
- Place the subject 70 px above centre: the Reels caption covers the bottom.
- Motion blur from keys at f−0.25, f and f+0.25, computed with that frame's own act, so nothing smears across a cut.
- **Seam math, not eyeballing:** after the render, export each part's projected 2D box per frame. Measure the spread
(the mean distance of the part centres from their centroid) across every act boundary.
- A jump over 2 px means a stutter. Fix it in the camera, not in the edit.

## 7. Render ★

- Run `--track` (timeline JSON) and `--track2d` (per-frame part boxes, depth, pass, field value). Then render all
frames with Cycles at 128 samples, adaptive threshold 0.03, OptiX denoise.
- Frames 0–11 are the hook: render them at 512 samples with threshold 0.01. Grain in the glass at 100 % is not acceptable.
- Render low-res tests of the extremes first (frames 0, 110, 200, 230, 262, 280). Judge the palette on its real backdrop
before spending the full render.

## 8. The vision layer (graphics in Python)

The graphics are diegetic: they are the machine's own readout, never captions or decoration. Composite them in numpy and
PIL over the raw RGBA frames.

- **Two backdrops only:** light for frames 0–11 and the clean beat, dark for the whole diagnosis.
- On light, the object casts a soft offset shadow plus a contact shadow.
- On dark, glowing parts spill a large, warm, blurred glow onto the ground.
- Add a touch of bloom and chromatic aberration, and one **static** grain texture (grain that changes every frame looks cheap).
- **Blend modes:** white vectors use **Exclusion**, so they invert what is under them; apply this to some elements, not
all. Over mid-grey, where Exclusion disappears, the ink is picked from the actual pixels under each label.
- **The safe band** (1080×1920): everything readable lives in y 250–1500 and clears the action column on the right
(x > 930 for y 1000–1500).
- **Type:**
- Fira Mono 24 / 28 for data, Space Grotesk 34 for part names;
- Regular weight only (bold reads cheap);
- 2 px lines, 4 px for the lead line.
- Labels never overlap: a placed label shifts, or it drops.
- **One lead graphic per act:**
- acquire: a dashed hull filling in;
- separation: multi-object tracking with velocity labels and short trails, plus a curved dashed node web;
- inspection: segmentation boxes on a 30 px grid, with the part names;
- core lock: crosshair, lock box, a thermal inset and a 1-bit dithered edge inset;
- reassembly: twelve rays converging on the seat point;
- working: the front line;
- limit: the alarm plate;
- recovery: the recovery front;
- clean: **nothing**.
- **Glitch with purpose:** datamosh, slice, RGB split or pixel-sort, only *inside* tracked boxes, held for 2–3 frames.
Never full frame. The bars must sample the part itself, never empty background.
- **Invert slap:** invert, then black and white, then contrast 1.5. Three frames on, three off, three on, at the separation,
the working start and the limit. **One polarity throughout:** the object as a white silhouette on black, graphics white.
- **Red belongs to the alarm.** It appears only after the limit is truly crossed. Everything else is white.
- **One scale for every number:** each temperature, pressure or load on screen is computed from that part's real field
value through one function, for example `T = min + (max − min) · v^1.6`.
- The legend, the insets, the log and the tags all agree.
- The limit act is the highest reading of the film.
- Parts the recovery front has passed read as recovered.
- IDs are consistent everywhere.
- **The log:** a typewriter with a scrambled leading edge, top left. Lines carry live values, not invented ones.

## 9. Sound (synthesised from the timeline, numpy only)

Three layers with roles:
- **mechanics:** impacts, the ejection roll, seat clicks, the lock;
- **machine voice:** the characteristic sound of [OBJECT] at work. Its pitch follows the real state curve from the
timeline, about two octaves over the working act;
- **data:** blips on log lines, ticks. Keep it about 18 dB under the other layers.

Events:
- a downbeat sound on frame 0;
- the separation as a roll, with three accents on the largest parts;
- near-silence in the inspection;
- three pulses with the core lock;
- a reversed swell into the lock at frame 168;
- one signature double hit for every slap;
- at the limit, a warning on its first beat and the alarm from the frame the limit is crossed;
- a release sound into the recovery;
- one soft air hit when the backdrop turns light.

Render the score twice in a row and keep the second pass, so tails wrap into frame 0. For phones, add harmonics so the
low end survives small speakers, and keep everything under 200 Hz centred. Master with gain plus a limiter to −14 LUFS
integrated and −1.5 dBTP. Check the mono fold-down.

Also write `deliver/cues.csv`: time, frame, bar.beat, event, what. Someone may want to redo the sound by hand.

## 10. Finish and delivery

- Encode with an explicit BT.709 conversion (`scale=out_color_matrix=bt709:out_range=tv`) and write all three colour tags
into the stream (`h264_metadata` bitstream filter). Untagged files shift gamma on phones.
- Deliver:
- `*_ig.mp4`: two-pass H.264, 16 Mb/s, AAC 320k;
- `*_master.mp4`: CRF 15;
- `*_clean.mp4`: the same film with no graphics and no slaps, for clients;
- `audio/`: the mix and its stems;
- `cues.csv`;
- five 4K stills (hook, close-up, limit, recovery, clean), composited on their own backdrops;
- a 1080×1920 cover that holds up as a 3:4 grid crop.

## 11. Quality gates (measure them and report the numbers)

1. **Seams:** spread jump ≤ 2 px at every act boundary; the reassembly spread decreases monotonically.
2. **Loop:** the object's bounding box on frames 287 and 0 matches within 2 px. Only the material changes at the loop.
3. **Flashes:** at most 3 full-field luminance flips in any second (aim for far fewer).
4. **Compression:** re-encode at 720p and 2.5 Mb/s, as the platform will, and check that every label is still readable.
5. **Safe band:** draw the Reels UI zones over six frames; no readable element inside them.
6. **Truth:** read every number on six frames aloud against the story. A reading that contradicts the picture is a bug.
7. **Taste:**
- one hero per frame;
- nothing static for long;
- nothing jittering at random;
- no green;
- no red before the alarm;
- no text outside the HUD;
- no logos.

Finish with a short report: the files, the measured gates, render time and anything you could not verify.
