2108199183983497433.prompt:
You're directing a 20-second animated short about the Claude Haiku 5.5 release. You're the director, the art department, the animator, the sound designer and the QA team, and you have real tools to call.

I'm giving you the idea, the tools and the quality bar. Everything else, from the beats to the look to the jokes, is yours to design. I trust your taste more than a beat sheet I could write. Your capabilities are far beyond what you assume, so work like it: plan carefully, push the craft, and use the tools and the time this deserves. Spend generously where it improves the film and economically everywhere else.

Final output: `out/level3.mp4`, 1920×1080, 30fps, exactly 20.0 seconds, with voices, music and sound design. At the end, you'll also save your process as a reusable skill.

---

## 1. The idea

**Opus is overloaded with work it shouldn't be doing.** It's buried in small, repetitive tasks: summaries, classifications, lookups, compactions. Then it has a realization: it can hand all of that to Haiku. It calls Haiku, Haiku arrives fast and clears the pile, and Opus is finally free to do the hard, important work it's built for.

That's the premise. How you tell it is up to you: the staging, gags, rhythm, camera, character beats, what the eureka moment looks like, how Haiku arrives, and how the delegation plays out. Sonnet can appear if it earns its place.

**Fixed points:**
- 20.0 seconds, 16:9.
- Opus and Haiku are characters in the same family as the Claude character.
- The film must read with the sound off.
- The ending respects reality: Haiku takes the volume, and Opus keeps the hard thinking. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 remain the better choice for complex agentic coding, so Haiku is never shown replacing Opus.

---

## 2. Style reference

The reference is Jake Moran's "Animated agent session story": https://www.prompt-motion.com/jake11moran-a269c4. It was made with this skill: https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes-community-skills/tree/master/skills/session-story. Read the skill, including its references on motion and the room.

Take from it:
- The hand-drawn watercolour-on-paper look.
- A cozy room as a world.
- Cartoon blocks with faces as characters.
- Physical paper props that carry the story (paper planes as tasks).
- A score that's cued to every action.

Don't copy it. Use it as a starting point and push it further: richer staging, better acting from the characters, more cinematic camera, and a stronger hook. It should look like it belongs to the same family, made by someone who studied it closely.

---

## 3. Facts (lock these before any creative work)

Fetch https://www.anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5-5 and write `facts.json`: every claim you might use, each with the exact supporting sentence from the page. Only claims in `facts.json` may appear on screen or in dialogue.

This is a story first, so use one or two facts at most, woven into the world rather than presented as slides. For example, a price tag being re-stamped, or Haiku's speed shown rather than stated. The film must end on a card with **Claude Haiku 5.5**.

---

## 4. Audience and hook

The audience is AI and developer Twitter/X: people who use Claude every day and know the model names and the jokes about them. Before writing the treatment:
- **Research:** spend a little time on how people currently talk about Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, and what's being said about this launch. Find one or two references or running jokes this audience would recognize and enjoy. Use them only if they fit the story naturally. Never use real people or brand logos.
- **The hook:** the first second has to work as a still frame on a busy timeline. Someone scrolling should instantly see "a character drowning in work" and want to see what happens.
- **Text on screen:** this is motion design that tells a story, not a lyric video. Use text sparingly and only where it adds something: a beat the picture can't carry alone, the fact stamp, and the end card. Integrate it into the world (painted, stamped, written in marker) rather than overlaying it.

---

## 5. Tools

The keys are in `.env`. Pick the best tool for each job, and tell me which you chose and why.

| Tool | Key | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Web search and fetch | — | Source page, style reference, audience research |
| Higgsfield (connector) | — | Image generation; call `models_explore` first to pick the best model for flat illustrated characters. Also music or sound effects if its audio models are the best fit. |
| GPT Image (OpenAI) | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | A second image model. Test both on the same prompt and keep whichever matches the style better. |
| ElevenLabs | `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | Character voices, sound effects, and music (Eleven Music) |
| Remotion | — | The film itself |
| ffmpeg + Python | — | Audio analysis, frame extraction, checks |
| Subagents | — | Parallel research and independent review |

---

## 6. Order of work

### Step 1: Treatment
Write `treatment.md`:
- Your take on the story in one paragraph.
- The beat sheet with timings.
- What happens in each shot: camera, acting, the gag.
- Where the music hits.
- What each character says.
- Which fact appears and how.
- Why this version is the strongest way to tell it.

Write two or three distinct treatments, then pick one and explain why.

### Step 2: Style bible
Write `style/bible.md`:
- Palette: 6 colours maximum, with hex values and a reason for each.
- Ink line rules: weight, and the "boiling" redraw jitter.
- Watercolour and paper texture.
- Lighting.
- Type: local font files only.
- Character design rules for Opus and Haiku: size ratio, shapes, how each one moves, and their expression set.

### Step 3: Key art (images as the base, no video generation)
The generated images are your key frames and design references. You are the in-betweener. Generate:
1. **Style frames:** 3 options of the world. Pick one.
2. **Character sheets:** Opus and Haiku, each with front, three-quarter and side views and their full expression set. Use the chosen style frame as a reference so everything shares one world.
3. **Key poses:** one image per key pose in your treatment (roughly 6–10), each built from the character sheets and the style frame, matching the camera and composition of the shot.

Put everything on one contact sheet.

**Stop and wait for my approval** before building anything.

The images are references. The final film is drawn in code to match them, and generated images never appear on screen. Trace the shapes, poses, proportions and composition from the key art into SVG, and animate between them.

### Step 4: Audio first
The film's timing comes from the audio.
1. **Voices:** audition at least 2 ElevenLabs voices per character. Opus should feel warm, low and deliberate. Haiku should feel quick, bright and eager. Generate each line separately, with 2 takes, and keep the best delivery.
2. **Music:** generate a track that fits your treatment, about 22s long, with its structure matching your beats: for example, a drop when Haiku arrives. If the generated track won't land on your beats, trim and offset it with ffmpeg rather than changing the picture.
3. **Sound effects:** a sound for every physical action. Paper, whooshes, impacts, the lightbulb, stamps.
4. **Timing map:** detect the music's beat onsets and write `timing.json`. It holds every beat time, the drop frame, each voice line's start and end frames, and every key action snapped to the nearest beat. All animation timing reads from `timing.json`, with nothing hardcoded.
5. Play me the audio-only mix before building the picture.

### Step 5: Build in Remotion
- **Components:** one per character, prop and set piece. Story beats live as data in `story.json`.
- **Drawing:** watercolour fills via SVG turbulence and displacement filters, a multiply-blended paper texture, and boiling ink lines.
- **Motion craft:** anticipation before every big action, follow-through after, squash and stretch, springs for landings, arcs for every moving object, and no linear easing.
- **Acting:** the characters have to perform. Give them readable poses, holds where the audience needs to read a face, and timing that's funny.
- **Mouths:** mouth shapes driven by the voice track's loudness. They must be still when the character is silent.
- **Camera:** push-ins, a whip or a shake where it helps. Motivate every camera move.
- **Mix:** music, voices and sound effects on separate layers. Duck the music under dialogue.

---

## 7. Verification loops (do not skip any)

1. **Key-pose match:** at every key pose, render the frame and compare it side by side with its key art. Write what differs and fix it.
2. **Sound-off read:** render a silent cut. A fresh subagent that has seen nothing else reviews a contact sheet at 2 frames per second and retells the story. If it can't, the staging failed. Fix it and repeat.
3. **Sync check:** list every catch, landing, stamp and dialogue line with its actual frame vs its `timing.json` target. Everything must be within 1 frame.
4. **Fact check:** every word on screen and in dialogue, matched to `facts.json`. Cut anything unmatched.
5. **Technical:** duration exactly 20.0s, stereo audio, peaks below −1 dBFS, no unintended dead air.
6. **Director's review:**
- Watch the whole film at least twice as frames.
- Write a brutal critique as the most demanding motion designer you know: what feels assembled, what's slow, what doesn't land.
- Fix the top 3 issues, then review again.
- Only then hand it over, with a 10-frame contact sheet.

---

## 8. Package it as a skill

Save the full pipeline as `.claude/skills/launch-film/SKILL.md`, so that next time *"Make a launch film for [URL] about [idea]"* is enough.

The skill should include:
- The fact lock
- The treatment process
- The style bible as a reference file

2114477295574425988.prompt:
Create a high-energy 16:9 music video using both supplied video clips, edited to exactly match the full duration of the supplied music.

EDITING:
Analyze both clips and the soundtrack. Select the strongest moments, creatively cut, interleave, rearrange and combine footage from both sources. Build a cohesive, fast-paced edit driven by the music's rhythm, energy, transitions and emotional progression. Freely alternate between clips, create visual connections and synchronize key actions with musical accents. Avoid simply playing the clips sequentially.

GRID STRUCTURE:
Use a dynamic, asymmetrical manga-inspired panel layout with large dominant panels, narrow strips, tilted rectangles and smaller supporting panels separated by clean white gutters. Use the reference image strictly for panel geometry, not its artwork or visual style. Mix moments from both clips across different panels, creating coordinated compositions. On major beats, dynamically rearrange panel sizes, positions and boundaries.

VISUAL EFFECTS:
Blend aggressive style infections spreading between neighboring panels with temporal variations, motion echoes, frame repetitions, time offsets and impact freezes. Create dense, layered visual effects, rhythmic flashes, graphic symbols and cross-panel chain reactions. Synchronize everything precisely to the soundtrack.

CREATIVE DIRECTION:
Let the footage and music guide all editing decisions, visual treatments, effects and transitions. Be bold, experimental and visually inventive. Keep the original characters, actions and environments clearly recognizable. Use large panels to maintain visual clarity while smaller panels explore creative variations. Effects should enhance the footage rather than replace it.

AUDIO:
Preserve the original audio from both clips, including dialogue, sound effects and ambience. Retain relevant sounds from the selected moments and mix them naturally with the supplied music. The soundtrack drives the edit and plays uninterrupted from beginning to end.
No typography, text, letters or numbers.

2105922894924501283.prompt:
Postav mi video, které vysvětluje pravidla sportu stylem televizní analýzy s AR grafikou. Bez AI video modelů a bez stahování assetů: 3D scénu, postavy, textury, grafiku i zvuk vytvoř kódem. Pracuj samostatně a průběžně mi ukazuj kontrolní snímky.

## Parametry (pro jiný sport změň tuhle sekci a sekci Scénář)
- Sport: fotbal
- Pravidla (9): ofsajd, faul, pokutový kop, vhazování, rohový kop + kop od branky, hra rukou, přímý volný kop, žlutá a červená karta, gól (celý míč za čarou)
- Jazyk všech textů: čeština (plná diakritika, desetinná čárka)
- Délka: cca 68 s (úvod ~4,5 s, každé pravidlo 6 až 8 s, závěr ~4 s)
- Formát: 1920×1080, 30 fps, MP4 (H.264 + AAC)
- Styl postav: PS2 éra ve stylu GTA San Andreas (low-poly tvarované tělo, ručně malované textury)
- Týmy: Červení (červený dres s bílými lemy, bílé trenky), Modří (královsky modrý dres, tmavě modré trenky), rozhodčí černý s limetkovými lemy, brankáři zelený a fialový

## Technologie a pipeline
- Three.js (npm). index.html obsahuje WebGL canvas 1920×1080 a nad ním DOM vrstvu pro HUD.
- Deterministická funkce `window.renderFrame(t)`: stav scény i HUD je čistá funkce času, žádný stav mezi snímky.
- `render.mjs`: lokální statický HTTP server + puppeteer-core se systémovým Chrome (headless, na Macu `--use-angle=metal`). Pro každý snímek zavolej renderFrame(t), počkej 2× requestAnimationFrame, udělej JPEG screenshot a pošli ho rourou do ffmpeg (libx264, CRF 18, yuv420p). Režimy: `stills t1 t2 …` (PNG na kontrolu), `video`, `info` (zapíše časovou osu do out/timeline.json).
- Cesty řeš přes fileURLToPath (složky s mezerami v názvu).
- WebGLRenderer s `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`, ACES tone mapping, PCF soft shadows. EffectComposer s MSAA (samples 4, HalfFloat): RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, vlastní grade pass (vinětace, jemné zrno, chromatická aberace, záblesk, whip blur, VHS efekt), OutputPass.
- Zvuk: Python (numpy + scipy) syntetizuje celý soundtrack do WAV, ffmpeg ho přimíchá (AAC 192k).
- Výstupy: plná kvalita + webová verze (CRF 23 až 24, maxrate 10M).

## Struktura projektu
src/util.js (easing, tmap pro freeze a zpomalení, track() pro pohyb hráčů po časovaných waypointech s fází běhu podle uražené vzdálenosti, seeded rng), src/world.js, src/player.js, src/ar.js, src/hud.js, src/grade.js, src/segments.js, src/main.js, render.mjs, https://audio.py/, PROGRESS.md (průběžně zapisuj, co je hotové a jak se to pouští, ať se dá navázat po přerušení).

## Svět
- Hřiště 105×68 m. Tráva jako canvas textura (pruhy po 5,25 m, šum, skvrny) + dlaždicová detail textura přes onBeforeCompile. Čáry jako ostrá geometrie, ne textura. Vnější hrana čar = hranice hřiště.
- Branky se sítí (LineSegments), rohové praporky.
- Stadion: dvoupatrová mísa podle superelipsy, dav jako canvas textura lidí v řadách, LED pás mezi patry, střecha s žebry, řady reflektorů na hraně střechy (emisivní, bloom), vnější fasáda s osvětlenými okny, noční obloha, světla města kolem, tmavá zem.
- LED mantinely kolem hřiště s českými nápisy (PRAVIDLA FOTBALU, RESPEKT, FAIR PLAY, ZNEJ PRAVIDLA, #PRAVIDLAFOTBALU), pomalu se posouvají.
- Světla: 4 směrová světla z rohů střechy se stíny (shadow kamera zaostřená na akci daného segmentu), hemisférické světlo, jemná mlha.
- Analytický grade: do všech materiálů světa vlož přes onBeforeCompile sdílený uniform uFreeze (odbarvení do chladné šedozelené + ztmavení). AR materiály ho nemají, takže při zastaveném obrazu zůstanou syté.

## Postavy (styl GTA San Andreas)
- Hierarchický rig: root → body (pánev) → trup → hlava a ramena → lokty, kyčle → kolena → kotníky. Póza = sada úhlů (náklon a rotace trupu, flexe a abdukce ramen, lokty, kyčle, kolena, kotníky, náklon těla, výskok).
- Geometrie: trup jako LatheGeometry (široká ramena, užší pas), zúžené končetiny, klouby jako koule, dlaň s palcem, kopačka s podrážkou a zúženou špičkou, tvarovaná hlava (užší brada), nos, uši, vlasy jako slupka (krátké, objemné, ježek, holá hlava).
- Ručně malované canvas textury: obličej (oči s duhovkou a odleskem, obočí, stín nosu, rty, tváře, strniště nebo vousy, vlasová linie), dres (V-výstřih, boční pruhy, znak, sponzor, jméno a velké číslo na zádech, vrásky látky), rukávy, trenky s číslem, štulpny s pruhy.
- Každý hráč jiný: pleť, vlasy, účes, oči, vousy, barva kopaček, postava. Česká jména na zádech (NOVÁK, DVOŘÁK, RŮŽIČKA…).
- Procedurální běh (fáze z uražené vzdálenosti, ať nohy nekloužou) + knihovna póz: kop (nápřah, úder, dokopnutí), skluz, zakopnutí a pád, vhazování, výskok s paží nad hlavou, zvednutá karta, postoj ve zdi, výskok zdi, robinzonáda brankáře, hlava dolů.
- Zvýraznění: obrysová slupka (inverted hull, tloušťka podle vzdálenosti od kamery), průsvitný hologram „ducha“ pro naznačení restartu, rozsvícení paže.

## AR grafika (additive blending, depthWrite false, kreslí se postupně přes progress)
GroundLine (zářící čára na zemi), Curtain (svislá rovina: ofsajd, branková a postranní čára), GroundRing (prstenec nebo disk s pulzem, čárkováním a výsečí, třeba kruh 9,15 m), Area (vyplněné území s okrajem a skenem), Trail (trubice trajektorie míče), GroundArrow (šipka s běžícími chevrony), Marker (zaměřovač kontaktu), Beam (světelný sloup), ScanGrid (skenovací mřížka), Segment3D (měřicí úsečky), Silhouette (válec obrysu těla).
Barvy: tyrkysová = měření, červená = přestupek, jantarová = míč a území, zelená = platné rozhodnutí.
DŮLEŽITÉ: shadery musí být NaN-safe (clamp UV, žádné pow ze záporného čísla). MSAA na hranách extrapoluje UV a NaN se v bloomu rozleje do černých bloků přes půl obrazu.

## HUD (DOM, styl sportovního přenosu)
- Logo vlevo nahoře „PRAVIDLA FOTBALU / AR ANALÝZA ZÁPASU“ + počítadlo „01 / 09“.
- Vpravo nahoře stav (ŽIVĚ, ZÁZNAM, ZPOMALENĚ ×0,6, STOP · AR, PŘETÁČENÍ ◀◀, KONEC ZÁPASU) a herní čas.
- Lower third vlevo dole: číslo pravidla, název, jednověté vysvětlení, ukazatel postupu z 9 dílků.
- Panel rozhodnutí vpravo dole v barvě rozhodnutí (OFSAJD, PENALTA, GÓL…) s podtitulkem.
- Při zastavení obrazu: záblesk, rohové závorky, štítek „ZASTAVENÝ OBRAZ · AR ANALÝZA“, krátký technický řádek dole.
- AR štítky ukotvené na 3D bod (projekce kamerou) s odkazovou čarou. Drž je v bezpečné zóně (ne pod spodní grafikou, ne pod logem) a nesmí se překrývat.
- Velká grafika karty (žlutá a červená) s důvody, úvodní titulek, závěr „TEĎ ZNÁŠ PRAVIDLA.“ s mřížkou 9 pravidel, stinger přechod (šikmé pruhy navy, tyrkysová, bílá + logo) na každém střihu.
- Čitelnost: minimální velikosti (název pravidla 66 px, popis 29 px, štítek 33 px + podtitulek 21 px, technický řádek 22 px). Text vždy na tmavém podkladu, krátké texty. Line-height aspoň 1,05, aby diakritika (Ž, Č, Ř) nebyla oříznutá. Titulky neodhaluj maskou, vypadá to jako ořez: použij fade + rozostření + lehký zoom.
- Fonty: systémové s českou diakritikou (na macOS DIN Condensed + Avenir Next Condensed). Pokrytí znaků ověř předem přes fc-query.

## Scénář (vnitřní časy segmentů, natažení na čtení viz další sekce)
Úvod (3,5 s): dron sjíždí z noční oblohy přes střechu do stadionu na široký záběr středu hřiště. Skenovací mřížka přejede hřiště, pod hráči naskočí kroužky, štítek „MÍČ SLEDOVÁN“. Titulek „PRAVIDLA FOTBALU“, nad ním „TV ANALÝZA PRAVIDEL“, pod ním „9 KLÍČOVÝCH PRAVIDEL · AR ANALÝZA“.
1. Ofsajd: televizní kamera, Červený #8 přihrává, zastavení v okamžiku přihrávky. Kamera se přesune do osy ofsajdové linie. Tyrkysová rovina u nejzazší části těla předposledního obránce (Modrý #4), červená u předsunutého kolena útočníka (Červený #9), měření „+1,59 m“ (spočítej z kloubů, paže se nepočítají). Rozhodnutí OFSAJD: nepřímý volný kop, Modří.
2. Faul: záznam ×0,6 nízko u trávníku. Modrý #10 vede míč, Červený #6 jde skluzem zezadu do kotníku. Zastavení v okamžiku kontaktu: zaměřovač „KONTAKT“, „MÍSTO FAULU“ (kruh + sloup), šipka dráhy skluzu, červený obrys. Kamera obkrouží, pak pád. FAUL: přímý volný kop.
3. Penalta: Červený #9 ve vápně, Modrý #3 ho podrazí. Zastavení, jeřáb nahoru. Zvýraznění pokutového území, oblouk z místa faulu na pokutovou značku s drátěným míčem, „11 m“. PENALTA.
4. Vhazování: přihrávka Červeného #2 přejede postranní čáru (trajektorie se kreslí živě). Zastavení až ve chvíli, kdy je celý míč venku, střih na kameru za čarou. Červená rovina, „+15 cm“, „CELÝ MÍČ VENKU“, „POSLEDNÍ DOTEK · ČERVENÝ #2“, modrá šipka do hřiště a hologram modrého hráče s míčem nad hlavou. VHAZOVÁNÍ (Modří).
5. Roh + kop od branky: střela Červeného #10 tečovaná Modrým #4 za brankovou čáru → ROHOVÝ KOP. Pak efekt přetáčení (VHS) a stejná střela bez teče → KOP OD BRANKY (zvýrazněné brankové území).
6. Hra rukou: střela, Modrý #5 ve výskoku s paží nad ramenem, míč do předloktí. Paže zčervená, ramenní linie, čára paže „ÚHEL PAŽE 135°“, průsvitný válec „OBRYS TĚLA“. RUKA: přímý volný kop.
7. Volný kop: zeď na 8,00 m „ZEĎ MOC BLÍZKO“, nakreslí se kruh 9,15 m, zeď ustoupí, číslo naběhne na 9,15 m a zezelená. Kamera za exekutora, zahraný oblouk přes zeď zpomaleně, zastavení „PŘES ZEĎ“. PŘÍMÝ VOLNÝ KOP.
8. Karty: detail rozhodčího se žlutou kartou proti hráči se svěšenou hlavou + velká grafika ŽLUTÁ KARTA / NAPOMENUTÍ se 3 důvody. Střih, červená karta, vyloučený odchází + ČERVENÁ KARTA / VYLOUČENÍ.
9. Gól: střela, brankář vyrazí, míč padá na čáru. Kamera u brankové čáry. První zastavení: polovina míče na čáře, červená rovina, „−11 cm“, „ZATÍM NENÍ GÓL“. Míč se dokutálí. Druhé zastavení: celý míč za čarou, rovina zezelená, „+3 cm“, blesky foťáků v hledišti. GÓL.
Závěr (2,5 s): kamera stoupá nad hřiště (návrat k úvodnímu záběru), mřížka, „TEĎ ZNÁŠ PRAVIDLA.“ + mřížka 9 pravidel, stmívačka.

Každé zastavení obrazu: krátký záblesk, odbarvení scény, kamera se dál pomalu hýbe kolem zmrazených hráčů, AR prvky naskakují postupně. Mezi segmenty vždy stinger.

## Čas na čtení
Akce (běh, kopy, skluzy) běží ve skutečné rychlosti. Analytické části každého segmentu natáhni 1,5× až 2,1× přes warp funkci (výstupní čas → vnitřní čas segmentu), aby každé pravidlo bylo na obrazovce 6 až 8 s a všechny texty se daly v klidu přečíst. `node render.mjs info` exportuje výslednou časovou osu do out/timeline.json.

## Zvuk (procedurální, https://audio.py/)
120 BPM broadcast groove (kopák, virbl, hi-haty, basa se sidechainem, arpeggio, pad), riser v úvodu, závěrečný akord. Při zastaveném obrazu hudba ztlumená low-passem. Dav (filtrovaný šum s vlněním, řev při gólu), whoosh + boom na každém střihu, kovový úder na každém zastavení, krátké „razítko“ při rozhodnutí, píšťalka, kopy do míče, zvuk přetáčení. Časy všech zvuků načti z out/timeline.json, ať sedí na obraz i po změně délky. Cílová hlasitost kolem −14 LUFS.

## Postup práce a kontrola
1. Nejdřív rozjeď pipeline (server, render, ffmpeg) s jednou scénou a ověř, že WebGL v headless Chrome běží.
2. Po každé změně vyrenderuj kontrolní snímky v klíčových časech a prohlédni je, včetně výřezů na 100 % kvůli textu a diakritice.
3. Celé video kontroluj přes kontaktní listy (ffmpeg filtr tile) a snímky kolem přechodů.
4. Hotové video ověř dekódováním (`ffmpeg -v error -i video.mp4 -f null -`) a délku a stopy přes ffprobe.
5. Do PROGRESS.md průběžně zapisuj, co je hotové a jakými příkazy se to pouští.

1. 冒頭：和紙の巻物が上から広がり、墨で描かれた配置図が現れる（題字・落款つき）
2. 図面の線が墨のワイヤーフレームとして立体に立ち上がる

5. 最後にタイトル【題材名】を表示

■ 描写（リアル寄り）
- 樹木・植物は、枝ぶりと葉の1枚1枚が見える作りに（球の塊にしない）

- 空は物理的な空。時間帯は夕方の低い日差しで、影を長く

- 外部素材なしでPython合成。場面の切り替わりに合わせた和風BGM＋効果音

■ 進め方
- テスト静止画を確認してから本番レンダリング
- 完成したらMP4で送って

2119772039037014524.prompt:
Create a 2D anime short. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Build everything in three.js (WebGL2) in the browser, render every frame headless in Chrome with a painted-background brush pass and an ink pass, and encode with ffmpeg. Deliver one 1920x1080, 24 fps MP4 with an orchestral soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

REFERENCE
Retell the final fight and the Serious Punch from episode 12 of One Punch Man shot for shot: the same actions, staging, camera angles, lens feel and timing. Redesign every visual from scratch, so the scene is recognisable only by what happens, never by how anything looks. 78 seconds, 31 shots.

WORLD
A shining city on a ring around a planet: towers of white coral with coral, apricot and celadon accents, hanging gardens, a pale esplanade with a balustrade, and a sea of clouds far below. Above the north of the city hangs a 7 km hive ship with ribs like a whale skeleton.

CHARACTERS
The hero is a calm capybara janitor in overalls with a straw broom and a small citrus on his head. The villain is an insect warlord in wine-coloured armour set with gems, who sheds that armour for a mantle of lime energy.

STORY
A quiet morning. The capybara sweeps one small pile of leaves while a lime beam cuts a trench through the district behind him, and he does not notice. A sky-tram pod plants itself beside him. The hive ship arrives. The warlord lands, boasts, and is ignored; the broom taps its toe. One slash cuts the skyline on a single straight line. The armour bursts. A barrage, a rush, a blade strike: the esplanade becomes a crater and he is left on a pillar, black with soot, yawning. He flicks the warlord apart, it regrows, rises and drains the sky into a spiral around a star. The wind finally takes his pile and the citrus falls from his head. For the first time in the film he looks up. One sweep of the broom: the sky is hollowed out, the ship breaks and the clouds open around the whole planet. The last leaf lands. He goes back to work.

LIGHT
Every shot has its own light rig: key, rim, bounce and one energy light with a visible source. High-key noon, ochre dust after the landing, a drained indigo sky under the star, then the cleanest air of the film. Impact frames in negative, white and ink with lime. Textures at several scales that fade with distance.

MOTION
Living bodies move with weight: centre of mass over the feet, no foot sliding, anticipation, overshoot, arcs, breathing, characters animated on twos.

SOUND
Real orchestral samples (CC0), mood decided second by second: a calm morning, dread when the ship arrives, minor brass and percussion through the fight with every hit on picture, total silence before the sweep, and the first major chord of the film only after it.

TEAM
Parallel agent departments, each owning its own files: city, sky, warlord, capybara, FX, sound. A shared map and shot list keep them in sync.

CHECKS
Before the final render a script tests every frame on the real geometry with BVH: no character, hand or foot inside the ground, props or another body; the camera never enters a mesh or goes below ground; feet do not slide; no camera jerks; nothing appears or vanishes in the middle of a shot.

2105927781678747965.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (one lowercase word, it becomes a black wordmark with a period), the one job a user hands it before bed, the three results it reports by morning, two photos of the same place at night and by day (aligned, so a crossfade reads as a real sunrise), one sunny daytime photo for outside the logo, and a song with a big hit near its start. If I skip any, use the defaults: "nightshift", "book 10 sales calls this week", 200 leads found / 200 emails sent / 10 calls booked.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 24 second square product launch video, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take that loops. The whole video happens inside the period of the wordmark. Outside it's daytime (the sunny photo behind a black wordmark). Inside it's the night photo under iOS-style glass panels (the blurred photo behind each panel, a tint, a rim light). Nothing cuts: every scene grows out of the last, shapes morph, dots fly, colours change under floods. Every morph glides 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve. Geist, the real macOS pointer, soft shadows that grow with each shape's height.
Banned: flat or gradient backgrounds made in code, camera zooms into tiny points, hard cuts, crossfades between scenes, bouncy springs, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, cropped type.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's. The song enters on its big hit as the first pill appears.
Open: the letters slide into the period and vanish into it while it glides to the middle. The period opens like an iris onto the night inside it, and "you log off at 6", then "[product] doesn't", roll through one mask line over the night photo.
Ask: a glass "Ask [product]" pill springs in. The cursor clicks it, it glides into an input and the job types out.
Find: send shrinks the input to a dot that ripples into a 23x15 grid. A scan line sweeps it, 200 dots light up and a counter counts them.
Write: the lit dots pour into a glass email composer. A second, purple cursor labelled "[product]" types a personal opener and presses Send, and the counter runs to 200/200.
Night: the composer becomes a glass orb with a progress ring. A clock chip swaps 11:42 PM, 3:17 AM, 5:02 AM, 6:59 AM while the sky relights from night to dawn and "while you sleep" rolls in.
Results (beat 20): the orb turns black and goo-splits into the three result pills. The checks pop green.
Morning: the pills merge into a Dynamic Island that grows into a phone lock screen: the day photo, the date, a big 7:00, the bezel growing out of the screen edge. Three glass notifications stack in, and the cursor taps the first, which opens like iOS.
Proof: a week calendar (10 meetings pop in, a hover shows one's time), then a pipeline chart ($48,200 counts up, the line draws, a hover follows it). A black flood from the line's end becomes "Start your night shift →" and the cursor clicks it.
Out: the button shrinks into a dot, the whole scene closes down into it like an iris, and the letters slide back out of the period. The tagline rises. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. One element morphs through every state (size, radius, colour, material) from a table of beat times, so retiming is one edit.
3. Render the inside world into an offscreen canvas and reveal it through the period with a circular mask. Never zoom the camera into the dot.
4. Glass: a pre-blurred copy of the photo clipped to the shape, then a tint and a gradient rim.
5. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merge.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. The song enters on its hit. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes. Scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.
</build>

<gotchas>
A camera zoom into an off-centre dot swings sideways and spikes, so open the dot instead. Ease a closing iris by area, not radius, or its first frames jump. A helper that sets globalAlpha must restore the caller's, or fading cards pop. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's, or the digits smear.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, find, write, results, phone, out) before you render.
</start>

2103757767727255661.prompt:
帮我做一条 30 秒的 2D 动画分镜预演短片《雨站》，要标杆级画质。不装 HyperFrames/Remotion，全部自己写代码（Python + ffmpeg）完成。

故事（24fps，2.39:1，4K）：雨夜高架站台。她穿米色风衣、撑透明伞，站在近侧站台；对面路灯下站着他，穿深灰长大衣、围围巾。
1. 0–6.4s 透明伞雨珠特写 → 后拉，焦点移到对面露出他（过肩镜头）
2. 6.4–9.4s 他的中近景：低头 → 抬头看向画左
3. 9.4–12.4s 她的正面近景：眨眼 → 认出他；远处传来鸣笛
4. 12.4–17s 远景：车头灯光先到，5 节列车驶过；第一个车厢缝隙里他还在，第二个已经空了
5. 17–18.8s 她含泪的近景，车窗光带扫过她的脸，头发被风吹起
6. 18.8–22.4s 尾灯远去，对面站台空了；他那盏灯闪几下后熄灭
7. 22.4–28.6s 她的背影，焦点从空站台拉回她；身后脚步声，一把黑伞遮到她头顶，她回头看向镜头；男声“好久不见。”，配字幕
8. 28.6–30s 黑场片名“雨站 / RAIN STATION”

做法：
- 原画：用GPT Image 2.5 画远景、他、她、列车（头车/中车/尾车）。人物一律用纯绿 #00FF00 背景，自己抠像（带参考图要透明背景会得到假棋盘格）。同一角色的各个姿态放在同一个会话里，以基准图为参考连续编辑；换姿态时只合成变化的区域。
- 画质：用 Real-ESRGAN x4plus anime 6B（HF 上的 safetensors 版，自己写 RRDBNet，跑在 MPS 上）把全部原画放大 4 倍；用 Depth Anything V2 估算远景深度，做逐像素视差。
- 渲染：自己写 2.5D 合成器。各层按真实深度摆放，针孔相机按真实焦距运动；做圆形焦外光斑、焦点转移、3D 雨丝、列车运动模糊、体积光、泛光和胶片光晕、细颗粒、调色。人物用网格变形做呼吸、风吹发梢、伞抖，关键姿态按日式“一拍二”切换。4K 超采样，逐帧缓存到磁盘，分 3 个进程按时间段并行（16GB 内存）。
- 声音：Mixkit 真实音效（雨、伞面雨声、列车、鸣笛、脚步）；按剧情节点写谱，用 Logic/GarageBand 自带的施坦威钢琴和弦乐采样渲染；台词用 Kokoro 中文男声；按镜头做声音远近，响度 -16 LUFS。
- 每一步都渲染预览帧、拼成图自检，修好再出片。交付 4K 母版和 1080p 分享版。

summary.zh: 这条30秒风格化2D分镜短片《雨站》由 Opus 5.5 调用 GPT Image 画原画、Real-ESRGAN 超分、Depth Anything 估深度，再用自写的 Python+ffmpeg 渲染器合成画面和声音输出，作者贴出了完整的长提示词。

2111814234090693110.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to transform into (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, no cuts: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a quick blur.
A cursor controls every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist).
Springs everywhere, with only a tiny overshoot. The camera zooms so each state fills the entire frame. The last frame matches the first frame, so it loops perfectly.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs expand into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is calculated from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
Springs use closed-form step responses. A value that changes targets multiple times is the sum of one spring per change, so it remains a pure function of time.
The tab indicator's two edges follow different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Use the same trick for the toggle knob.
Drags use direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is calculated from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
Analyze the song with numpy to find the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Position every UI sound by its measured peak.
Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or difficult to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text becomes blurry.
Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps.
Make the final frame identical to the first, including cursor position and speed, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before writing any code.
</start>

summary.zh: 一段完全用代码渲染而非After Effects制作的UI动态设计循环视频，基于作者公开的Claude Opus 5.5结构化提示模板（规定UI状态、弹簧动画和节拍同步剪辑），使用Playwright和ffmpeg渲染。

2112189854234652746.prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (Three.js via CDN, no other assets) that is the 2026 version of the "ball bouncing inside a spinning hexagon" test.

Scene: a large hollow hexagonal prism (a 3D hexagon) slowly spinning on two axes at once. Inside it, a smaller hexagonal prism spins the opposite way, and inside that, a tiny one. Three nested spinning cages. The cage walls are see-through panels drawn only as clean outlines with a very light flat tint, so every ball inside stays clearly visible.

Physics (write your own, no physics library):
- Start with 1 ball inside the innermost cage. Every 2 seconds a new ball spawns, up to 300, each with its own random size, mass and color.
- Real gravity, friction, restitution and spin. Balls must collide with each other and with the rotating walls, picking up the wall's velocity at the contact point so they get flung realistically. No tunneling through walls, no jitter when balls rest on each other.
- When a ball hits a wall hard enough, that wall panel cracks and eventually breaks into flat shards that also obey physics, so balls can escape into the next cage outward.
- The outer cage never breaks. Escaped balls pile up at the bottom of it.

Look, clean cel-shaded style:
- Toon shading on everything: 2 or 3 hard shading bands per object, crisp dark outlines (inverted-hull or edge detection), flat colors from a small tasteful palette.
- A plain flat light background (soft off-white or pale gray), with a simple flat floor shadow under the cage.
- No bloom, no glow, no neon, no lens flares, no motion blur, no particle haze, no gradients, no transparency stacking. No visual artifacts: no z-fighting, no flickering outlines, no shadow acne, no aliasing (use antialiasing and a sensible pixel ratio).
- Impacts get small, flat cartoon "pop" marks that vanish quickly, not sparks.
- It should look like a clean animated illustration, not a tech demo.

Camera: a slow, smooth orbit by default, plus drag to orbit and scroll to zoom.

Sound: synthesize everything with the Web Audio API. Each collision makes a soft pitched tone based on ball size and impact speed, so it turns into gentle generative music as it gets chaotic. Breaking panels get their own sound. Keep it quiet and pleasant, never clipping.

UI: a small, minimal flat panel in the corner (no glassmorphism) with sliders for gravity, spin speed, bounciness and ball count, a "slow motion" toggle, a "reset" button, and an FPS counter. It must stay at 60fps with 300 balls on a laptop.

summary.zh: 一个由Claude Opus 5.5根据详细提示词生成的自包含HTML/Three.js物理模拟，展示球体在相互反向旋转的多层六边形笼子中弹跳，带有卡通渲染风格、可破碎墙体和基于Web Audio的生成式音效。

2119554953018773795.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the product (a real one I give you, or invent a fake brand so there are no brand issues), the genre the story hides inside (detective, alien invasion, heist, nature doc, cooking show), and where it will be posted (it decides the follow handle). If I have no idea, pitch me 3 "What if" stories that each hide the product inside a genre, and let me pick. Ask which voice tool I have: ElevenLabs (about 1,000 credits a Short) or free Kokoro run locally. Tell me no image or video model is needed, because every frame is drawn in code. Then show me the script with word counts and seconds per line, a rough storyboard, and a cast sheet before anything costs money.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 60 fps, 40-45 s vertical Short: a 2D "What if" kid cartoon that is secretly an ad, drawn entirely on an HTML canvas in code. Not 3D, not AI images, not a Roblox look. It borrows the big What-if channels' rhythm (DAY/CASE cards, a HUD counter, poofs, pop-in captions, a rewind loop) but every character and outfit is original.
The ad formula (from the best Pixar-style AI ads):
- Cold open in a genre with no product mention for the first beats; the viewer thinks it is a story.
- The product enters as a plot device (the evidence, the stolen thing, the reason someone wins), never as an ad.
- The twist is the product's benefit turned into a punchline ("too good to share", "too hard to kill").
- End on one glossy packshot: the product spinning in on a sunburst with a 2-line tagline.
Characters: short, chibi, cartoony, one shared rig for the whole cast.
- Big round head (radius 150 at scale 1, slightly wider than tall), small pear-shaped body, stubby rounded legs and arms ending in round mitten hands, oval shoes with a coloured sole. Adults are taller (1.2-1.3x body), little siblings 0.82x.
- Every shape has an 8 px #2a1b3d outline and one soft darker shade on its right edge only (a thin crescent, never half the face).
- Hair is smooth rounded shapes: a cap that covers the whole crown, a soft side swoop, a bowl cut, a side part, a ponytail hanging BEHIND the head. Never spikes or zigzags.
- Give every character their own outfit; never copy a reference creator's character clothes 1:1. Example cast: detective kid (tan belted trench coat, red scarf wrap, brown fedora with a band), little brother (red-white striped tee, blue overalls, bowl cut), Mom (black hair, yellow headband, ponytail, coral sweater, green pants), Dad (side part, short jaw beard, round thin glasses, green sweater vest, white shirt, blue tie), dog (white with a brown eye patch and floppy brown ears).
- Faces carry the comedy. Eyes: normal (white with a big pupil and two highlights), huge, happy arcs, closed, star, spiral, narrow. Brows: up, worry, angry, flat (mirror them per eye so worry never reads as angry). Mouths: smile, grin, wide, scream (one clean open shape with teeth band and tongue), o, flat, smirk, wavy, chew (puffed cheeks). Plus blush, sweat drops and sunglasses that drop in. Blink for 0.1 s about every 1.6 s. Mouths flap only while that character's words are being spoken.
Sets: detailed flat rooms in saturated colours with thick outlines, each with a night version (darker blue grade plus warm lamp glows): a kitchen (wallpaper, upper cabinets, window with curtains and sky, jar shelf, plant, clock, pendant lamp, tiled backsplash, drawer counter, checker floor) and a bedroom (striped wall, window, poster, toy shelf, bed with a star blanket, nightstand lamp, plank floor, rug). Bursting sunburst colours for montages and the packshot.
Fonts (all free, from Google Fonts' GitHub repo):
- Captions: Lilita One.
- Day/CASE cards and big world words: Luckiest Guy.
- The product wrapper text: Sniglet ExtraBold, auto-fitted so it never clips.
Captions:
- 1-2 words at a time in Lilita One 94 px, centred at y 1600 (on the legs, never across a face), max 900 px wide.
- White with a 20 px #1c1030 outline and a soft shadow, popping from 55% to 100% in 0.16 s.
- Key words in caps and colour: red #ff5165, green #5dff8f, yellow #ffd23f, pink #ff7ad9, cyan #7debff, orange #ffa53d, purple #c49bff.
- No full stops or commas on screen, ever. Hide captions on the packshot.
Fake game UI over the world:
- A HUD counter pill (260x92, centred at x 540, y 196) with a tiny product icon that tracks the story (snacks stolen, clues found) and ticks with a green "+N".
- CASE/DAY cards: Luckiest Guy 230 px in yellow #ffd23f with a 38 px outline, tilted -6 degrees, popping in over 0.22 s and leaving at 1.05 s.
- Toast pills (88 px tall at y 374), a FOLLOW button with the handle chip and a cursor that presses it (it turns green "FOLLOWING").
Motion: something moves on every line, and the picture changes every 1-3 s.
- Things arrive with a squash (0.72, 1.12, 0.95, 1 over 0.3 s), an overshoot ease or a white poof cloud with stars, never a plain fade.
- Characters breathe (1.2% squash) all the time.
- The camera pushes in 5-15% per shot, stays inside the set, and shakes (decaying over 0.35 s) on every hit.
Banned: real logos or real creators' characters, AI stills, spiky hair, a frame that holds still for more than 1 s, captions over faces, system fallback fonts, whispered narration.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 40-45 s, 85-100 words, 14 lines. Times below are from the 40.3 s "Snack Detective" ad; key every beat to a real word.
0-5 s: the narrator reads the title as line 1 ("What if you were a detective and someone kept stealing your snacks?") over the striking picture (crime-scene tape round an empty drawer; the hero poofs in on "detective"; the drawer slides open empty).
5-8 s: the hero's line that proves it ("My Krunchkin bar! GONE!"): spiral eyes, scream, a toast pill ("CASE OPENED"), the HUD appears with +1.
8-13 s: CASE 1. Suspect one (little brother with chocolate on his face, a magnifier finds it) and a tiny excuse line ("It's paint!").
13-17 s: CASE 2, bigger. HUD +1. A second suspect (the dog) looks guilty, the wrapper slides out.
17-21 s: CASE 3, the biggest. HUD +3. A third suspect (Dad "on a diet", a bar in his pocket) with a callback pop-in of suspect one pointing.
21-24.5 s: the follow beat told inside the story ("Follow, and the detective gets one more clue"): the button is pressed about 0.5 s into the line and a clue card drops in.
24.5-26.5 s: the turn begins ("So you set a trap"): night, a spotlight on the product as bait.
26.5-29 s: a 3-shot montage with no voice (0.85 s each on bursting colours): DUST!, NIGHT CAM (green tint, REC), RING RING! The counter races to 999.
29-30 s: the hero's line ("Got you!"): flashlight snaps on. The music cuts dead.
30-35 s: the twist: the fridge light floods on, it is Mom, chewing ("They're too crunchy to share, sweetie"), sunglasses drop in.
35-37.5 s: the packshot ("Krunchkin. Too good to share."): the bar spins in, crumbs fly, TOO GOOD / TO SHARE pops in.
37.5-39.8 s: a short tag from the hero ("Wait, there's a whole box?") as Mom slides a giant box into frame, HUD +94.
last 0.55 s: REWIND. The whole film scrubs backwards to frame 0 with scanlines and a REWIND label, so the end loops into the start.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (free): Python 3 with numpy, scipy and Pillow, FFmpeg, Node with Playwright and its Chromium, faster-whisper large-v3-turbo (int8 on the CPU), git for fonts. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Script and storyboard first:
- "you" and "your" point of view, the title as line 1, one picture per line, 10-16 words at most per line, words a 10-year-old uses, no names.
- Draw the storyboard with the real rig and real fonts (15 panels at 1080x1920, tiled with times, speaker and line), and a cast lineup. Zoom in on every character at full size and fix hair, hats, glasses, mouths and outfits before showing me.
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v3 with stock library voices, one take per character, all of that character's lines in one request separated by blank lines.
- Narrator: an energetic young male creator voice (Liam). Hero kid: a playful bright voice (Jessica). Mom: sassy (Laura). Little brother: the kid voice pitched up 3 semitones afterwards.
- Audio tags: [excited], [screaming], [nervously], [sweetly], [mischievously], [confused]. Write numbers as words ("Case one").
- Ask before spending credits. Check the API key's own credit cap before the big narrator request.
- Run faster-whisper with word timestamps on each take. Match lines by word count with difflib, refine each line's edges on the audio itself (pad 0.06 s before, 0.15 s after).
- Squeeze pauses inside a line to 0.22 s. Leave 0.2 s between lines, 0.33 s before each CASE line, and a 2.55 s silent slot for the montage.
- Level every take to the narrator's median. Word times on the finished track come from the take times plus the assembly offsets, so every cut, card, caption and sound starts on a real word.
4. Film (free): one HTML page with one canvas, where every frame is a pure function of time: https://window.seek/(t), window.READY, window.END.
- A SHOTS list of [start, end, function] keyed to word times (cuts land 0.04 s before their word). Each shot sets a camera (centre, zoom over time, clamped to the set), draws its world and characters, and the overlays (HUD, cards, toasts, follow button, captions) draw in screen space on top.
- One rig function draws every character from a pose: x, y, scale, squash, rotation, flip, arm and leg angles, head tilt, eyes, brows, mouth, look, blush, sweat, shades, prop. Hand positions come from the same arm maths, so props (magnifier, flashlight, product, salad, paintbrush) sit in the hand.
5. Check before render: contact sheets at the start and end of every line on the real timing. Fix captions over faces, props out of frame, cards over heads, camera past the set edge, and any text that clips.
6. Render (free): seek 120 subframes a second in headless Chromium, pipe JPEG screenshots to FFmpeg, blend pairs with tmix for motion blur at 60 fps (about 8 min for 40 s on 2 CPUs). Encode the upload copy with libx264 CRF 20, preset slow, AAC 256k (about 26 MB).
7. Sound (free, Mixkit):
- Music: one playful bed ("Comical"), about 19 dB under the voice. Cut it dead on the two big moments (the trap springing and the twist reveal), back on the packshot.
- Effects placed so each one's loudest moment lands on its frame: a poof on arrivals, pops and whooshes on cards, a coin ding on every counter tick, a glint on the magnifier, a boing on silly pop-ins, a slam on screams, a click and slam on the flashlight, a gasp and sting on the reveal, a crunch on the product, a party horn on the tagline, a rewind sound on the loop.
- Effects on speech 12 dB under the voice, in gaps 4 dB under. Measure voice versus everything else per line and duck the rest under any line below 15.5 dB (the worst line should end at 15.5 dB or more).
- Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1.5.
8. Final checks: no frame still for over 1 s outside a deliberate beat, captions on their words, and a look at 15 frames across the finished file before delivering.
</build>

<gotchas>
- My workspace's own internet is blocked; fonts come from Google Fonts' GitHub repo with a sparse git clone (ofl/lilitaone, apache/luckiestguy, ofl/sniglet). Never fall back to DejaVu or another system font.
- A browser tab can call ElevenLabs but cannot save files into my folders. Record the voices with a small .bat on my PC that curls the API into the project's Raw folder, and runs faster-whisper there in the same double-click.
- An ElevenLabs API key can have its own credit cap below the account balance. A refused request returns quota_exceeded; log the response body so the reason is visible.
- Whisper writes "1" for "one" and drops "!" and "..."; match lines by word count, not exact text.
- Spiky or zig-zag hair always looks broken. Use smooth bezier hair caps whose top reaches above the head's crown, or the crown shows as a bald band.
- A ponytail drawn in front of the body covers held props; hang it behind the head on the far side.
- Square glasses crash into the brows; use round thin rims centred on the eyes with the brows above them.
- A hanging scarf tail reads as a tie; use a neck wrap with a small side knot.
- Big shading ellipses split faces in half; keep the shade a thin crescent on one edge.
- Plain script tags share one global scope: a page variable named like a helper function (window.N vs function N) blanks the whole page. Prefix names.
- A zoomed camera centre near the floor shows black past the set edge. Clamp the camera centre to the set for its zoom.
- Captions at y 1290 and 124 px covered faces in every close-up; 94 px at y 1600 sits on the legs.
- Hits placed on screamed words ("GONE!", "box?") pushed the voice under 15 dB; check per line and duck before normalising.
- The follow beat is one swappable shot: change the handle per platform and re-render only that.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the product and the genre, or pitch 3. Then show me the script (word count and seconds per line), the storyboard and the cast sheet before any voice is generated.
</start>

2115393082472681875.prompt:
# Small animations for a product site's feature tiles

Give every tile in my site's feature grid a small animation: a tiny scene that shows what the feature does.

## 0. Before you build
- Read the project: find out the tech stack (plain HTML/CSS, React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind, Framer Motion…) and build it the way the project already does. Don't add an animation library unless the project already uses one.
- Ask me which look to use:
A. The Lumno material below, as written.
B. My product's own style: take the colors, radii, borders and shadows from my existing design tokens and components, and keep only the structure and motion rules from this prompt.
C. A mix: the Lumno material in my brand's accent color and radii.
- Picking features: if I named features, animate those. If not, read the product's site, docs or code, list 3–5 features that a short scene can explain, and let me pick.

## 1. Lumno material (option A)
Overall: quiet, neutral, precise. Hairlines instead of borders, soft shadows tinted warm, no gradients or color washes, one accent color.

- Grid: one card with an outer radius of 28px. Cells are separated by 1px hairlines (a 1px grid gap over a hairline color). Cells are white. The card has a faint hairline ring and a soft shadow.
- Art panel: inset 8px from the cell edge, with a radius of the card radius minus the inset (20px), so corners stay concentric.
- Fill #fafafa, plus an inner 1px ring: box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(32,38,46,.07).
- Texture: background: repeating-linear-gradient(-45deg, rgba(32,38,46,.06) 0 1px, transparent 1px 7px).
- The scene sits centred on the panel, about 126×118px.
- Text bars: body bars 4px tall with a 2px radius in #e5e9ef; heading bars 5px tall in #cdd4de. Vary the widths (34–92px).
- Mini windows and cards: white with a 9px radius.
- Shadow: 0 0 0 1px rgba(47,42,34,.06), 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(47,42,34,.25).
- Tab strip: 20px tall, #eef1f5. Tabs: 16px tall with 6px top corners; the active tab is white.
- Favicons: 10px.
- Inner surfaces such as charts or fields: #f4f6fa. Secondary data: #b9c9e0. Accent: #3462ad, used only on the result.
- Icon chip (top-left of each tile): 32px, 10px radius, 1px border rgba(32,38,46,.1), white, shadow 0 1px 2px rgba(32,38,46,.05), a line-style glyph in #4b5563.
- Text color: a warm near-black, #2f2a22.
- Hover: the cell darkens to about 2.5% grey; the panel goes to #f4f5f6 with its ring at .09; the icon chip grows 32→36px from its top-left corner, its glyph turns to the text color, and its shadow deepens slightly.
- Dark mode (suggested values; keep the same relationships):
- Cells #17181a, panel #1d1f22, inner ring rgba(255,255,255,.06), texture rgba(255,255,255,.04).
- Body bars #2c2f34, heading bars #3a3e45.
- Windows #24272b with a 1px rgba(255,255,255,.06) outline and a shadow of 0 8px 20px -10px rgba(0,0,0,.6).
- Tab strip #1a1c1f, accent #6f9bea, text #ecebe8.

## 2. Scene
- One idea per tile: 2–4 moves that show "action → result", such as "click → a small window opens" or "change here → the other side syncs".
- Abstract wireframes only: no screenshots and no real text. Use at most one small icon where something needs to be recognisable.
- Motion: ease-out for movement, cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1); a slight spring for appearing, cubic-bezier(.34,1.4,.64,1). Each move takes 250–600ms; the whole scene is done in about 3s.
- Icon chip: when the tile plays, its glyph redraws stroke by stroke (draw, pop or slide per part), then hands back to the solid icon.

## 3. Playback
- Resting styles are the final frame. Animations only describe where things come from (fill-mode: both or equivalent), so reduced motion shows the result and an interrupted play never jumps.
- The art panel fades in (opacity, plus translateY 6px and scale .97 to none) as its tile first plays.
- Play once in view: when about 70% of the tile is visible, wait ~200ms, then play. Tiles that enter together go ~250ms apart, in reading order. Stop on the final frame.
- One "played" state (a class or data attribute) drives every animation in the tile. To replay: remove it, force a reflow, add it back (or re-key in a framework).
- On mouse hover (mouse only) or keyboard focus, replay: blur the final frame out over ~160ms (blur 6px, opacity 0), restart under the blur, then clear it. Don't restart a play that hasn't finished.
- Optional loop on hover: while the pointer stays on the tile, replay again ~600ms after each play ends. When the pointer leaves, finish the current play and rest on the final frame.
- Touch: a tap follows the tile's link; nothing depends on hover.
- prefers-reduced-motion: reduce: no animation; show the final frame.

## 4. Colors and dark mode
- Every color is a variable on the art panel (panel, ring, texture, bars, windows, tab strip, accent, shadow); no hard-coded colors in the rules.
- Follow prefers-color-scheme, and the project's manual theme switch too (a class or data-theme), if it has one.
- Check it in both light and dark.

## 5. Delivery
- Mark the art as decorative (aria-hidden) and keep translatable text out of it.
- Check it in a real browser: first play, hover replay, keyboard focus, reduced motion, dark mode and a phone-width layout.

2120124748159996152.prompt:
Ask me 2 things, then wait:
1. The story in one line: a strange TRUE event where one person did one odd physical thing ("He tied 42 weather balloons to a lawn chair."). If I say "you pick", pitch 3 with one source link each and take the first unless I choose.
2. The voice. Default: Kokoro (free, runs on my computer), a calm, warm male narrator.
Then tell me everything else is free: Blender (find my install, or tell me the one download), its free MPFB extension for human bodies (ask me before you install it) and into this folder a Python venv with FFmpeg (imageio-ffmpeg), kokoro-onnx + its model files (kokoro-v1.0.onnx and voices-v1.0.bin from the kokoro-onnx GitHub releases), faster-whisper (small.en), numpy and Pillow. It needs no API key or account and renders on my graphics card with EEVEE.
</inputs>

<direction>
The look: a clean, realistic 3D world, like a good game cutscene. Bright, saturated, a little filmic.
- People: realistic bodies with generic faces and big readable expressions (shock, a smirk, a scream). Plain clothes, no logos. Never a real person's likeness: for a real person keep the face out of close-ups (hands, back, side, distance, straight top-down).
- CALM shots only. Bodies in fast action or contact (running, jumping, fighting, falling) look stiff, so tell the story with frozen moments under a slowly moving camera, macro inserts of hands and objects, rooms, vehicles, the sky, top-down views and the aftermath.
- One new picture for every caption chunk (2-4 words, about 1-1.5 s): a new framing, a new action or a camera move. Nothing ever holds still: every shot drifts, pushes in or orbits.
- The shot kit: macro insert (extreme close-up of the key object or hands, very shallow depth of field), hero low angle (wide lens at waist height), god's-eye top-down with a slow rotate, tracked object, over the shoulder, smash zoom on the word that matters, whip pan between beats, glow highlight (the named object glows orange with a rim, then fades), a big 3D number lying in the scene, a thought bubble (a cloud ring showing what he hoped for), a TV in the scene replaying the event.
- Light: a bright warm sun, blue sky with clouds, soft shadows. Night scenes use hard lamps and a dark sky. Wide lens up close, depth of field on every shot, motion blur on every fast camera move.
- Captions: 2-4 words at a time, white bold rounded sans, about 64 px on a 1080 px-wide frame, centred, 78% down the frame, soft dark shadow, no box. Each chunk replaces the last on the same frame as its picture.
- Banned: real footage, photos, downloaded textures or 3D models, logos, AI images or AI video, downloaded music, gore.
</direction>

<structure>
38-50 s, 100-140 words, 150-180 words a minute. The voice starts at 0.0 s.
- Line 1: the most surprising physical act, in past tense, opening with "He" (or "She"). No name, date or setup. Frame 1 shows that act.
- Then a cause-and-effect chain: every sentence starts with a hinge word (Then, Suddenly, So, Because, But, Later) and is ONE visible action.
- The context arrives late, after "You see,".
- A reveal: someone looks closer and the story turns.
- The last line is the consequence. No call to action, no question.
- Names are rare: use one only when it pays off.
Title = "He ..." or "The Man Who ...". The cover is the first frame.
</structure>

<build>
Save every stage to disk so a crash never costs more than one stage.
- sources.md: every fact with its link and the date you read it. Anything you can't verify stays out.
- script.json: the lines and the caption chunks cut by hand (2-4 words, one picture each), each chunk with its shot: the set, the camera, what moves.
- https://voice.py/: Kokoro reads the whole script in one take (speed 1.0-1.1) and pauses are squeezed to 0.35 s at most; faster-whisper times every word (pass it a 16 kHz numpy array, not a path); write chunks.json with each chunk's start and end. A picture and its caption switch together on frame round(start*30)+1.
- blender/: Python scripts run headless (blender -b -P). https://build.py/ makes one .blend with the sets, the cast, the props and every shot baked with a key on every frame. https://look.py/ sets EEVEE with ray tracing, the AgX view with the Punchy look, motion blur, depth of field and bloom in the compositor. Bodies come from MPFB or are built by you; clothes, hair, props and sets are built in code.
- Stills first: one half-size still per shot as a contact sheet. Look at every tile and fix what's off before any full render. Time one full-size frame and tell me the estimate.
- Render 1080x1920 at 30 fps to PNG frames, skipping frames already on disk.
- https://sound.py/, numpy only: a light music bed, a sound on every action (a whoosh on each whip pan, hits, wind, room tone), ducked under the voice, mastered to -14 LUFS on the whole stereo mix.
- https://compose.py/: burn the captions in from chunks.json. Encode out/<slug>_9x16.mp4 (1080x1920, 30 fps, TV-range yuv420p) and out/<slug>_x_7x8.mp4 (1008x1152, under 10 MB, 2-pass): a crop of the 9:16 frame that keeps the subject and the caption.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Blender paths: pass absolute output paths (a relative one lands on the drive root).
- MPFB headless: enable it with addon_utils.enable("bl_ext.user_default.mpfb"). Bake a body's shape keys before you pose it: the rig is fitted to the baked shape.
- Clothes: cut them from the body mesh and push them 7-16 mm out along the normals; keep two rings of body faces under every hem.
- Nothing coplanar: keep every resting object 1 cm off its neighbour and draw ground markings into the texture, or they flicker.
- Hair: EEVEE draws hair only from a Curves object, hair type STRIP. Use a Principled BSDF on it (the Hair BSDF renders black).
- Skin: keep subsurface weight near 0.2 (more turns faces black in EEVEE) and add a soft fill light from below under a noon sun.
- Hands: a curled hand reads as a claw from the palm side, so shoot a grip from behind the knuckles.
- Motion blur: shutter position START, a key on every frame, plus a key half a frame after each shot's last frame, so blur never reaches across a cut.
- Check: run a black-frame and one-frame-flicker check on the render. Make a contact sheet (a frame every 0.5 s) and look at every tile: the act reads in the first 2 s, faces are lit, nothing clips through anything, captions stay off faces and key objects. Then step through the first 2 s, the middle and the end frame by frame. Fix, render only the changed shots again.
</gotchas>

<start>
Pitch (or take my story), then show me the script with the word count, the caption chunks with their seconds and the shot list with what the first frame shows. Build nothing until I say go.

Page : "Design World — Explore New Ideas". ================================================== 2. PAGE STRUCTURE (HTML) ================================================== <section class="hero" id="hero"> <canvas id="scene" aria-label="Rotatable glass cube. Drag to rotate."></canvas> <div class="ui"> <h1 class="sr-only">Explore New Ideas</h1> <header class="nav"> <a href="#" class="logo"><i class="logo-mark"></i><b>Design</b><span>World</span></a> <ul class="nav-links"><li><a>Home</a></li><li><a>Portfolio</a></li><li><a>Contact Us</a></li></ul> </header> <div class="arrows"> <button class="arrow" id="prev">[left-arrow SVG]</button> <button class="arrow" id="next">[right-arrow SVG]</button> </div> <nav class="dots"><button class="dot"></button><button class="dot active"></button><button class="dot"></button></nav> <p class="tagline">Let's Build the<br>Future of <strong>Design.</strong></p> <div class="cta-row"> <a href="#" class="cta">Explore Now</a> <span class="cta-line"></span> <span class="count" aria-hidden="true">07</span> </div> <div class="loader" id="loader">Loading model</div> </div> </section> Arrow SVGs: viewBox 0 0 24 24, fill none, stroke currentColor, stroke-width 2.6, round caps/joins. prev path: "M19 12H5M11 6l-6 6 6 6" next path: "M5 12h14M13 6l6 6-6 6" IMPORTANT: The big "Explore / New / Ideas" headline is NOT HTML text. It is drawn onto a 2D canvas inside WebGL so the glass cube can refract it (see section 4). The HTML only has a visually hidden <h1> for accessibility. ================================================== 3. CSS (exact values) ================================================== :root { --bg:#000; --fg:#fff; --pad-x: clamp(20px, 6.95vw, 120px) } html, body { height:100%; background:#000; color:#fff; font-family:'Poppins',sans-serif; border-radius:0 20px 20px 0 } /* white "D" half-circle */ .logo b { font-weight:700 } .logo span { font-weight:400 } .nav-links { display:flex; gap:clamp(20px,4.1vw,60px); list-style:none } .nav-links a { color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; font-weight:500; position:relative } .nav-links a::after { content:''; position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:-4px; height:1px; background:currentColor; transform:scaleX(0); transform-origin:right; transition:transform .35s ease } .nav-links a:hover::after { transform:scaleX(1); transform-origin:left } ARROWS (top-right, left of the dots column) .arrows { position:absolute; top:18.9%; left:76.7%; display:flex; gap:32px; transform:translate(-19px,-50%) } .arrow { width:38px; height:38px; border-radius:50%; border:2.5px solid #fff; background:transparent; color:#fff; display:grid; right:calc(var(--pad-x) - 7px); top:49.4%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:33px } .dot { width:14px; height:14px; border-radius:50%; border:2px solid #fff; background:#fff; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s } .dot.active { background:transparent } /* active = hollow ring, middle one active by default */ TAGLINE (bottom-left) .tagline { position:absolute; left:var(--pad-x); bottom:clamp(40px,7.5vh,70px); font-size:clamp(24px,2.65vw,44px); line-height:1.2; font-weight:300; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .tagline strong { font-weight:700; display:block } CTA ROW (button → horizontal line → giant outlined "07" bleeding off the right edge) .cta-row { position:absolute; left:45.6%; right:-1vw; top:88.7%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; align-items:center } .cta { flex:none; padding:0 15px; height:48px; display:inline-flex; align-items:center; border:1.5px solid rgba(255,255,255,.85); border-radius:6px; background:rgba(0,0,0,.15); color:#fff; font-size:14px; font-weight:400; text-decoration:none; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .cta:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } .cta-line { flex:1; height:1.5px; background:rgba(255,255,255,.8); min-width:40px } .count { flex:none; font-size:clamp(140px,19.8vw,360px); font-weight:400; line-height:1; letter-spacing:-0.02em; color:transparent; -webkit-text-stroke:1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.9); transform:translateY(6%); user-select:none } LOADER .loader { position:absolute; left:50%; top:50%; transform:translate(-50%,-50%); font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.2em; text-transform:uppercase; opacity:.6; transition:opacity .6s } .loader.done { opacity:0 } RESPONSIVE @media (max-width:900px), (max-aspect-ratio:1/1) { .arrows { left:auto; right:var(--pad-x); top:15%; transform:translateY(-50%); gap:14px } .tagline { bottom:clamp(150px,20vh,220px) } .cta-row { left:var(--pad-x); right:-3vw; top:auto; bottom:24px; transform:none } .count { font-size:clamp(120px,22vw,200px) } } @media (max-width:640px) { .nav-links { gap:16px } .nav-links a, .logo { font-size:13px } .dots { gap:20px; right:16px } .dot { width:10px; height:10px } .cta-row { right:-8vw } .count { font-size:120px } } @media (max-width:420px) { .nav-links li:nth-child(2) { display:none } } /* hide "Portfolio" */ No horizontal page scroll at any width. ================================================== 4. WEBGL SCENE (Three.js) ================================================== Renderer: WebGLRenderer({ canvas:#scene, antialias:true, alpha:false }), clearColor #000, outputColorSpace SRGBColorSpace, pixelRatio = min(devicePixelRatio, 2). Camera: PerspectiveCamera(fov 30, aspect W/H, 0.1, 100) at (0,0,10) looking at origin. 4a. Background headline (drawn into an offscreen 2D canvas → CanvasTexture) - Canvas size = viewport × DPR, filled #000. - mobile = (W < 768) || (W/H < 1). - fontSize fs = min(H*0.21, W*(mobile ? 0.21 : 0.118)); font = `800 ${fs}px Poppins`. If the widest line is wider than W*(mobile ? 0.9 : 0.5), scale fs down to fit. - Lines: "Explore", "New", "Ideas". Fill #e9e9e9, textAlign center, baseline alphabetic. - Centre x = W*(mobile ? 0.5 : 0.505); centre y = H*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.468). Line gap = fs*1.07; cap height ≈ fs*0.7. Line i (0..2) baseline y = cy + cap/2 + (i-1)*gap. - Texture: colorSpace SRGB, LinearFilter, no mipmaps. Redraw on resize and on document.fonts 'loadingdone'. - Show it with a fullscreen quad (PlaneGeometry(2,2), ShaderMaterial, vertex outputs position.xy directly, fragment = texture2D(uTex, vUv) followed by #include <colorspace_fragment> ON ITS OWN LINE; depthTest/depthWrite false; frustumCulled false) in its own bgScene. - Wait for fonts before first draw: Promise.race([Promise.all([document.fonts.load('800 100px Poppins'), document.fonts.ready]), 2500ms timeout]) then layout() + start loop. 4b. Model loading - GLTFLoader.load(MODEL_URL). Traverse gltf.scene; for each mesh: clone geometry, delete 'uv','color','tangent' attributes, mergeVertices(g, 1e-4), computeVertexNormals(), applyMatrix4(mesh.matrixWorld). Merge all parts with mergeGeometries. - Centre the geometry on its bounding box and scale uniformly so its largest dimension = 1. - Scene graph: scene → pivot (screen position + scale) → spinner (rotation) → cube mesh. On load add class "done" to #loader. 4c. Cube placement (in layout(), on load and on resize) - visH = 2*tan(fov/2)*10; visW = visH*aspect. - Screen-fraction centre: sx = mobile ? 0.5 : 0.517, sy = mobile ? 0.45 : 0.488. pivot.position = ((sx-0.5)*visW, (0.5-sy)*visH, 0). - On-screen edge length px = min(H*0.44, W*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.29)); pivot.scale = (px/H)*visH. - Initial spinner rotation: Euler(-0.42, 0.62, 0.18). 4d. Glass material — custom ShaderMaterial, screen-space refraction with 6-band chromatic dispersion, rendered in two passes (back faces, then front faces). Vertex shader: varying vec3 vNormal; varying vec3 vEye; worldPos = modelMatrix*position; mvPos = viewMatrix*worldPos; gl_Position = projectionMatrix*mvPos; vNormal = normalize(normalMatrix*normal); vEye = normalize(https://mvpos.xyz/); Fragment shader: uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / uResolution (drawing-buffer size). n = normalize(vNormal); if (uBackside > 0.5) n = -n; // do NOT use gl_FrontFacing, three.js flips winding for BackSide eye = normalize(vEye). LOOP = 16 iterations; slide = i/LOOP * 0.045. For each band compute refract(eye, n, 1.0/ior) with iorR/Y/G/C/B/P and sample uTexture at uv + refr.xy * (uRefractPower + slide*k) * uChromatic, with k = 1 (R), 1 (Y), 2 (G), 2.5 (C), 3 (B), 1 (P): r = tex(R).x*0.5 y = (tex(Y).x*2 + tex(Y).y*2 - tex(Y).z)/6 g = tex(G).y*0.5 c = (tex(C).y*2 + tex(C).z*2 - tex(C).x)/6 b = tex(B).z*0.5 p = (tex(P).z*2 + tex(P).x*2 - tex(P).y)/6 R = r + (2p + 2y - c)/3; G = g + (2y + 2c - p)/3; B = b + (2c + 2p - y)/3 color += vec3(R,G,B) color /= LOOP; saturation adjust: mix(luma(color), color, uSaturation) with luma weights (0.2125, 0.7154, 0.0721). Specular (Blinn-Phong, light vector = normalize(-light), view = -eye): spec = specular(uLight, uShininess, uDiffuseness) + 0.6 * specular(vec3(1,1,-1), uShininess*0.6, uDiffuseness*0.5) spec(x) = pow(max(dot(n,halfVec),0), shininess) + max(0,dot(n,lightVec))*diffuseness color += spec * (backside ? 0.35 : 1.0) Fresnel: f = pow(1.0 + dot(eye, n), uFresnelPower); color = mix(color, vec3(1), f * (backside ? 0.25 : 0.55)). color += vec3(0.004, 0.005, 0.007). gl_FragColor = vec4(color,1); then #include <colorspace_fragment> on its own line. Uniform values: uIorR 1.15, uIorY 1.16, uIorG 1.18, uIorC 1.22, uIorB 1.22, uIorP 1.22, uRefractPower 0.30 (front) / 0.22 (back), uChromatic 0.5, uSaturation 1.08, uShininess 90, uDiffuseness 0.02, uFresnelPower 5.0, uLight (-1, 1, 1), uBackside 0 (frontMat, side FrontSide) / 1 (backMat, side BackSide). 4e. Render pipeline (every frame) - Two WebGLRenderTargets sized to drawing buffer (W*DPR × H*DPR), type HalfFloatType, default (linear) colour space: rtBack, rtFront. - backMat.uTexture = rtBack.texture; frontMat.uTexture = rtFront.texture. 1) render bgScene → rtBack 2) render bgScene → rtFront, then (autoClear=false) cube with backMat → rtFront 3) render bgScene → screen, then (autoClear=false, clearDepth) cube with frontMat → screen - This gives the look: text seen through the cube is magnified, mirrored and split into blue/yellow fringes, inner rounded edges of the cube are faintly visible, and the bevelled edges glow white. ================================================== 5. INTERACTION & ANIMATION ================================================== - Drag to rotate (pointer events on the canvas, setPointerCapture): dx = Δx*0.008, dy = Δy*0.008; apply as world-space rotation: premultiply spinner.quaternion by axisAngle(Y, dx) then axisAngle(X, dy). Track velocity per 16.67ms frame; add class "dragging" to the canvas while dragging. - Inertia after release: keep applying velocity, damped by 0.94^(dt*60) per frame. - Idle drift: 0.6s after release, blend in a constant slow rotation of 0.0035 rad/frame around Y and 0.0012 rad/frame around X (blend ramps 0→1 over 1s). It also runs from page load. - Prev/Next arrow buttons: smoothly rotate the cube -90°/+90° around Y (ease: each frame apply remaining*min(1, 0.09*dt*60) until remaining < 0.0005). Cancels inertia; dragging cancels the spin. - Dots: clicking a dot makes it the only .active one (hollow ring). - Hover transitions: nav link underline wipe (.35s), arrow and CTA buttons invert to white bg / black content (.25s). - Clamp frame dt to 0.05s. Recompute layout (renderer size, camera aspect, render-target sizes, uResolution, headline canvas, cube position/scale) on window resize. ================================================== 6. LAYOUT REFERENCE (desktop 1440×806) ================================================== - Logo at (100, 38), 40px tall. Nav links right-aligned, right edge ≈ 1340, vertical centre ≈ 58. - Arrow circles centred at ≈ (1105, 152) and (1175, 152). - Dots at x ≈ 1340, y ≈ 351 / 398 / 445 (middle one hollow). - Headline "Explore / New / Ideas" centred at x ≈ 727, ~170px ExtraBold, baselines ≈ 272 / 445 / 637. - Glass cube occupies ≈ x 510–1000, y 145–600, slightly right of centre, overlapping the headline. - Tagline "Let's Build the / Future of / Design." at left 100, bottom ≈ 60px, ~38px, Light with Bold "Design.". - "Explore Now" button at (657, 691), 48px tall; a 1.5px line runs right to a huge outlined "07" whose "0" starts at x ≈ 1140 and whose "7" is clipped by the right and bottom edges. - Pure black background, all UI white. Mobile (≤767px or portrait): headline and cube centred at 50% x / 45% y, headline up to 90% width, arrows move under the nav on the right, tagline sits above the CTA row, and the CTA row is pinned 24px from the bottom with "07" partly off-screen on the right. Output: one complete index.html, nothing else.
